Issue body:
I'm trying to get this client to work for me but the fact that the UserManager expects a standard and fully-baked window object (with XMLHttpRequest), localStorage and sessionStorage (with getItem/removeItem makes it tough to develop Isomorphic react applications.

It would be great if the client did not assume/require a browser environment and could take a generic object as its store.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2016-11-02T12:30:18Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-257850963
Well, the description for this repo says "OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth2 protocol support for browser-based JavaScript applications" :)

But sure, if I knew what that was more, then I'd love to hear what support is needed. Is isomorphic a native framework for running JS & react?


Comment 2 | created 2016-11-11T20:50:15Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260052368
Isomorphic React isn't a framework. It just means writing your code so it runs both on the client and the server. The server obviously doesn't have things like localStorage/sessionStorage/cookies, at least not out of the box (there are many polyfills for Node to fill in some of this functionality, but they vary widely in quality and how recenlty they've been updated). So writing your library in such a way that it assumes those things exist means your library just can't be easily used isomorphically.


Comment 3 | created 2016-11-11T20:51:53Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260052719
The reason this is desirable is because it means that a React application can benefit from all the speed of a cached application on initial pageload, but subsequent interactions/routes/etc can be handled within the browser. In addition to performance benefits, it also has SEO benefits.


Comment 4 | created 2016-11-11T20:55:09Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260053358
React Starter Kit is just one of a number of boilerplate React projects that are isomorphic out of the box. https://github.com/kriasoft/react-starter-kit


Comment 5 | created 2016-11-11T20:57:08Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260053795
At any rate, it seems that you would want to give the user the option to use no browser-based storage of any kind, even if they aren't writing isomorphic applications. Concerns of personally identifiable information being what they, it seems you would want to give the user the option of passing in a simple in-memory object as a store.


Comment 6 | created 2016-11-13T15:02:54Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260191380
Sure, for storage that's extensible. Just implement the `WebStorageStateStore` API and set the `userStore` on the `UserManagerSettings`.

OpenCandy is considered adware [according to Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenCandy); in addition, I didn't even have to look it up to know what it was. Comment 1 | created 2017-02-16T20:07:13Z

Project: pupilfirst/pupilfirst

Issue number: 418

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 8/8
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
This is a feature that we haven't tackled so far because of its relative complexity. Instead of building this, we've always suggested that users take advantage of existing video hosting platforms such as YouTube and Vimeo to upload their video content and then _embed_ them inside targets. The argument has been that these platforms have done an enormous amount of work into making the video upload / hosting easy, fast, accessible, and cheap.

However, there could be use-cases where this isn't practical, and where the user would prefer that these large files be managed directly by the LMS. In almost all cases, these large files appear to be videos, and the use is to stream video content.

The main "pain" driving this feature appears to be the inconvenience of uploading videos to another service - It would be really nice to be be able to use Pupilfirst to directly manage video content - something that is frequently an integral part of a course's content. To me, this looks like a good problem to solve.

However, another major driver appears to be to disallow students from sharing or downloading videos to their local systems - as a form of _Digital Rights Management_. The issue with this, is that whatever measures we take, there will always be ways around it, and to a technically capable user such measure are merely inconveniences. I'm unsure as to whether this is a direction we should even attempt to take.

### Options that I can see:

1. Build the feature-set in-house. This means building a direct-upload system (Rails [has good support for this, as of v6](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/active_storage_overview.html#direct-uploads)), **and also** the content-delivery side of it; I'm unfamiliar with the complexities of global streaming delivery of video - I'm sure there are plenty.
2. Integrate with a third-party service to manage video uploads and content delivery. For example: [Cloudflare Stream](https://www.cloudflare.com/products/cloudflare-stream).
3. Build both - i.e., build a direct upload system to handle generic large files (but only allow simple "downloads" of these), and seperately, integrate with a video upload & streaming service to handle hosting of streaming video content.

Options 2 & 3 look preferable to me, but IMHO, more research is required here.

Comment 3 | created 2020-09-03T08:58:03Z

@Subomi I had a discussion about this with my team, and we're of the opinion that it would be best if the platform has as little involvement with the storage and handling of the video (and associated expenses) as possible. We propose an approach where school admins can upload videos directly to a Vimeo account that they own and manage.

### Proposed approach

1. Use [Vimeo's OAuth flow](https://developer.vimeo.com/api/authentication) to allow school admins to _connect_ their own Vimeo account to the school.
2. On the target content editor, if a Vimeo account is connected, enable a new _Video_ content block type.
3. When the block-type is selected, ask the user to pick a video file.
4. Send details of the video, including its byte-size to the Rails server.
5. At the server, use the video file details to [create a video at Vimeo](https://developer.vimeo.com/api/upload/videos#resumable-approach) - make sure to set `privacy.embed` to the school's known FQDN-s, and then return the `upload_link` and `uri` that was returned by Vimeo.
6. At the client, use the `upload_link` and an appropriate brower-based TUS library to upload the video file.
7. Once upload is completed and verified, use the `uri` that was supplied by Vimeo earlier with the existing embed flow to embed the Vimeo link.

### Why this approach?

1. This approach seems to involve the least amount of work. 😁 
2. School administrators retain full ownership of video content.
3. Vimeo's privacy controls ensure that videos can be played only via the school.
4. Moving to another service or platform is possible since Vimeo's API allows downloads of original content.

One aspect of this that can be seen as a disadvantage is that school admins need to get a subscription to _another_ service to make the `privacy.embed` feature work. However, the cheapest plan from Vimeo will allow this to work, and we think it's reasonably priced - it begins at an affordable USD 12 p/m or 84 p/y.

This flow should still work, even without a paid plan - I think that the `privacy.embed` feature would be the only thing that'd have to be left out if the connected account is on the _free_ tier.

@adesokanayo Correct. This isn't the _best_ option from a user-experience standpoint. What we're doing here is simply the most _reasonable_ / _achievable_ option that solves the biggest pain-points: namely: 1) the inability to upload videos straight from the LMS interface and 2) the inability to lock down the videos such that they can be played only on the LMS website.

Issue body:
Following Twitter, private accounts would display toots only to followers (not unauthenticated users or non-followers), and would require follow requests to be authorized by the user in question before they go through. This is something that's really important for marginalized users who want to escape not only active harassment, but the passive ability for hostile people to see into their lives.

I know that this is addressed in [the FAQ](https://github.com/Gargron/mastodon/wiki/FAQ#what-about-private-accounts), but I'm hoping this issue can stand as a place for users to express support for the feature and for progress to be tracked, however long it takes.

Comment 1 | created 2016-11-22T08:44:36Z
Source: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/180#issuecomment-262180573
It looks like GNU social at least notionally supports both of these features within a single instance, [as described in the FAQ](https://gnusocial.net/doc/faq#faq-20). Even if supporting federated followers of private accounts takes longer, it would be really great to have per-instance privacy in the short term.

Comment 2 | created 2016-11-22T10:17:20Z
Source: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/180#issuecomment-262201322
I do understand the importance of private accounts. However, I am opposed to solutions that only work within a single instance. It means that all your friends from other servers would have to switch to yours to see your posts, and that runs counter to the idea of federation.

Comment 3 | created 2016-11-22T12:04:00Z
Source: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/180#issuecomment-262223931
It seems to me the fact that privacy is inherently restrictive makes it a little more palatable—you could even imagine someone setting up their own Mastodon node with stringent requirements for registration, and setting their visibility to node-only on purpose.

That said, I do understand your hesitation. What about this as a compromise: support federated privacy controls, but have the UI gracefully degrade across nodes. Specifically, between two nodes:

* Any request for non-public information about a protected user, or actions on that user, results in a 403.
* *In addition* to the above, a request to follow a protected user shows up in their UI as a follower request.
* If the protected user approves the follower request, the prospective follower's requests no longer 403 (even though they aren't following yet).
* If the requester follows and then unfollows the protected account, they lose access to it again.

This requires an extra iteration on the follower's part, but it's properly federated and requires no protocol changes. It could also be cleanly folded into the protocol by simply having the publisher's node send a notification to the subscriber's node saying "your follow request has been approved", which would cause the subscriber's node to re-issue the follow request.

Comment 4 | created 2016-11-22T12:30:35Z
Source: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/180#issuecomment-262228840
The way subscriptions work (PubSubHubbub) is this:

- Account have public Atom feeds that link to a hub
- You can send a subscription request to the hub for that feed
- When the account publishes something, it notifies the hub
- The hub takes the public feed, takes new items, and delivers them to all subscribers

The hub is independent from the rest of the application, so if a feed is not public, the hub won't be able to deliver it to anyone.

This could be solved by piggybacking "private followers" on the Salmon protocol instead of PubSubHubbub. Salmon is for delivering signed notices to individual accounts (like "alice followed bob" being delivered to bob), but you could technically send private statuses to followers that way. It would, however, at least currently, be incompatible with GNU social. Most importantly, there is no protocol for saying "this feed is private, send a follow request first".

(Quite ironically because there is a follow request verb/activity type in the ActivityStreams protocol iirc)

To sum it up, it's not impossible, but it would take exploring new frontiers rather than simply implementing existing protocols.

Released issue metadata:
Issue title: A flexible approach to privacy and location
Project: openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['anonymization']"
GitHub labels: ["enhancement", "Provider"]
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 9; discussants: 6
Reported: 2018-09-12 18:46:16+00; last active: 2020-10-22 18:06:00+00
Issue number: 61

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 9/9
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
The MDS technical workshop made clear that LADOT wants precise location data as part of their interactions with providers. LADOT feels that can manage any real or perceived privacy risks that stem possessing anonymized, location-precise trip data, and that the benefits of this data are significant. 

From comments made at the workshop, it seems that there is not universal agreement on this point, especially given the variability in state-level FOIA laws and the different attitudes individual cities have about the broad topic.

I'd like to propose that MDS be extended to allow for flexibility in how location data is reported for trips and routes. LA can choose to require precise data, but other jurisdictions would have the flexibility to request less detailed information. It is ultimately a policy decision, and a universal spec needs to support some level of policy variance across its users.

Two approaches to (intentionally) reducing the accuracy of GPS data:

1) Blurring data to report less precise coordinates. These would correspond to a radius of uncertainty (e.g. accurate to within 500m).

2) Aggregating data into defined boundary areas (e.g. census block, ZCTA, neighborhood, etc.).

Option 1 seems like the simplest approach. It could be done without change to the MDS specification. Providers and agencies would simply agree on the level of specificity in the route's GeoJSON FeatureCollection. With this approach, the specification can simply be modified to acknowledge the possibility of deliberately imprecise data and leave it up to the stakeholders to agree on the details.

Option 2 may be easier for cities to consume (since they're already used to aggregating data into boundaries like census block), though would necessitate more pre-processing by the providers. It also would require modification to the specification since GeoJSON does not have an obvious way to describe location within specify externally-defined boundary areas.

Thoughts on:

1) Whether we should modify the spec to support imprecise location sharing?
2) If yes, what method to use?

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2018-09-12T19:54:52Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-420776349
Nitpick: I think that option 1 would require a small change to the spec in that you’d need to remove the line:

> Additionally, routes must include all possible GPS samples collected by a provider.

I vote option 1. It’s much more flexible and allows for accurate routes for providers and agencies who are comfortable with that. I suspect that many agencies will want to know traffic patterns, and that is only discernible via option 1.

Note too that a provider and agency could agree to implement option 2 with the spec of option 1 by just saying that the provider will move each point to the center of its census block (or neighborhood or whatever). The converse (implementing option 1 with the spec of option 2) is not possible. 

Also, I’d argue that option 2 is worrisome given that there is no international block/neighborhood standard. 

Comment 2 | created 2018-09-12T20:42:24Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-420790455
This is a great discussion. We've heard reports of certain vendors truncating their values to 2 decimal places already! At least, LADOT should be clear they are requiring 6-7 decimal points in latitude and longitude values, without snapping.

I don't believe that truncation is an appropriate anonymization technique, but a snapping technique that is related population-density (like census tract) might be. However, such low-precision locations are not useful for street-level insights, as @aickin points out.

Comment 3 | created 2018-09-12T22:21:49Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-420817415
Agreed with @ezheidtmann, great discussion on this topic!

I think the proposal over at #51 would actually cover @jfh01's Option 1 above, correct? 

Comment 4 | created 2018-09-12T22:32:02Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-420819952
I think it would. I don't think we need a way to reflect GPS accuracy separately from intentional "deprecisioning." 

As @ezheidtmann points out though, there's a larger question about whether this approach can achieve a good balance between utility and privacy. The answer may end up being dependent on the needs/attitudes of each city.

There's a related question on time-specificity. One additional privacy measure would be to provide trip data with the start and end times rounded to the nearest 15 minute or 1 hour increment.

Comment 5 | created 2018-09-14T20:21:06Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-421473807
A good article on the specific risks with geo-precise, anonymized data:

https://research.neustar.biz/2014/09/15/riding-with-the-stars-passenger-privacy-in-the-nyc-taxicab-dataset/

Even without persistent user IDs, there is some risk of reidentification or misuse.

Comment 6 | created 2018-09-19T02:30:24Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-422627060
A little late to this thread but option 1 seems like a good option. It's worth distinguishing between accuracy and precision. What we are really recording with `accuracy` is "precision" even if we provide 12 decimal places due to limitations of GPS the accuracy of those readings will probably be less because of factors that effect GPS like urban canyon.

Good  [StackExchange thread](https://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/8650/measuring-accuracy-of-latitude-and-longitude) on the subject.

Comment 7 | created 2018-09-19T18:55:54Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-422919215
I agree that we don't want to conflate imprecision due to the fundamentals of GPS sensors (called `accuracy` on both major smartphone platforms) with intentional lowering of precision via truncation or snapping. 

Imagine a tool that processes MDS entities -- that tool should be able to know whether it's working with a stream of GPS locations, a list of census tract centroids, or a list of locations snapped to a 1km grid. (just 2 examples)

Comment 8 | created 2019-05-21T23:32:45Z
Source: https://github.com/openmobilityfoundation/mobility-data-specification/issues/61#issuecomment-494596911
Could one version of the specification just take block level aggregations to a [SharedStreets ](https://github.com/sharedstreets/sharedstreets-ref-system) ID or OSM ID? I realize this is an old thread but, I think this provides the degree of operational data many cities would need for curbside management and related applications. I think route choice applications might be lost, but this might be a problem that requires a tiers of deployment perhaps?

I agree with @aickin  that this could be compatible with by snapping all points to the the nearest "centroid" of a SS ID or OSM ID. Benefit of these is that in theory they should be able to be internationally compatible if based around OSM. 

My only concern here is it might not be "anonymized" enough.

Comment 1 | created 2018-05-27T18:49:27Z

The last few weeks, we were pretty busy ensuring the DSGVO-readyness for Incloud. In this process, we created a whitepaper for our clients that summarizes what needs to be done in order to get their web applications DSGVO compliant: https://www.incloud.de/files/EU-DSGVO-Whitepaper.pdf

In a nutshell:

- Easily understandable privacy policy.
- Possibility to export all the personal data, that GELI has saved for my account.
- Possibility to fully delete my own account.
- Anonymization of all the personal user data, that is not needed in order to operate the platform. Maybe IP addresses that are sent to Google Analytics?
- Regular security updates of all the used libraries and of the operation system itself to ensure the system is as "hacking proof" as possible.

Issue title: trust in administrators issue
Project: benadida/helios-server
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['anonymization']"

Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
I came across a possible issue with Helios and I wanted to know your opinion.
In helios/models.py there is this code

```
  def compute_tally(self):
    """                                                                                         
    tally the election, assuming votes already verified                                         
    """
    tally = self.init_tally()
    for voter in self.voter_set.exclude(vote=None):
      tally.add_vote(voter.vote, verify_p=False)

    self.encrypted_tally = tally
    self.save()
```

it  loops over the votes, and add them using homomorphic encryption.

It seems to me an administrator can, when the election is closed, run a modified copy of the code, on the production database, and filter the voter_set to include only the user that he wants to de-anonymize (the information in the records). Helios will compute an election result including only the vote of that person, thus de-anonymizing the vote. The operation can be repeated for every voter. 

This exploit allows de-anonymization without breaking the homomorphic encryption. This will allow  de-anonymization at any time and by anybody who has access to the db after the election is closed.

Is there anything in Helios that would prevent a database administrator from being able to do this?
If not, I believe this should be clearly stated in the documentation that trust in the system administrators is required.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2017-06-10T00:14:09Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307528280
@mdipierro if I understand correctly, it would be better to store the votes on the election and not on the individual voter, yes?

Comment 2 | created 2017-06-10T01:42:13Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307534046
It is more complicated than that. Helios allows people to change their vote which means there is a link between the voter identity and the encrypted vote. This link exists and it is a feature. The encrypted vote can be added to the tally without decryption therefore nobody can see before it is added to the tally. My claim is that it can be see after it is added to the tally. A modified version of the code, or third party script, acting on the production database can be constructed to add the vote of a single user to an empty tally and this allows to know the vote of that specific user. I do not know how other systems handle this. I can tell you have eVote prevents this. In eVote the ballots are created when the election starts and put in their own table. When a voter arrives, a random ballot is picked and used. There is no link in the database between the voter and which ballot the voter has used. For this reason we do not even timestamp when voters vote. Two attacks are of course possible in both eVote and Helios: collusion between the email sender and database administrator, continuous monitor of database changes. I think both can be prevented by locking access to the server during voting or simply logging server activity during voting. The problem presented in this thread is in my opinion more serious because it can be exploited at any time. It is hard to tell who will get ahold of the database in the future, in particular if it is not run in house and deleted after the election. I do not believe the problem is solvable and keep the feature that voters can change their vote. Maybe I am wrong and I have overlooked something.

Comment 3 | created 2017-06-10T15:10:05Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307570801
@mdipierro with a single server authority, there is no known way for any system to solve the problem you mention. Sure, you can use access control to lock down server access, but if you're worried about an evil server, how do you know what source code it's actually running? You can get pretty far down that rabbit hole.

The only known way to solve this from an information theoretical point of view is to have multiple election trustees, where a majority is needed to perform decryption. If that's the level of security you want – and some organizations do, of course – then you can do that with Helios by creating additional trustees. Then decryption requires all of them to be involved, and the concern you have goes away.

If you don't want that overhead, Helios still provides a lot of voter privacy protection: only a clearly malicious server administrator could get access to the votes. It's not like peaking at a database. And Helios still allows you to have complete logs of who voted when, which has proven itself to be incredibly important for debugging typical errors that occur in elections.

Hopefully this helps. Happy to continue the discussion.

Comment 4 | created 2017-06-10T15:24:56Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307571686
First of all, thanks again for Helios. I learned from it.

My recommendation is to add an option to Helios that makes it behave like evote in this respect. My My recommendation is this: Create all ballot records in advance and, when a use shows up to vote, record that vote (like you do now) but on a random unused ballot and do not store anywhere the link between that ballot and the voter. Do not even store then timestamp when the vote is casted. You would lose the ability to change your vote but at least for me, that is not as a big issue as real anonymity.

To be clear the concern is not the trust in the people who run the election at each one time. It is more subtle. With eVote, once the election is closed, the db can be made public. I think in any election, once the ballots are counted, all the records should be made public so that people have confidence in the system. As it is, in Helios, the database cannot be made public. Anybody who gets ahold of it would be able to break anonymity. The database my leak. The next sysadmin may not be as trusted as the current one. It does not matter that Helios does not include the code to do it. I may publish an exploit to do it I wanted to do it.

I think Helios is great in may respect and I think there are many organizations that will be fine using Helios despite this problem. I think it would be appropriate to mention this issue in the web page, when talking about anonymity.

Comment 5 | created 2017-06-10T15:28:07Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307571880
@mdipierro if we did this – unlink voter from vote – then it would be trivial for the administrator to add an extra vote to the tally and *change the result* without any publicly auditable trace. So that seems a good bit worse, and in fact your goal would then not work: publishing the database wouldn't really provide any confidence around the tally.

If you want to publish the database with Helios, there's actually an easy way: delete the private key. Everything still checks out for public verifiability, and decryption is no longer possible.

Comment 6 | created 2017-06-10T15:32:39Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307572153
The way we solve this in evote is to publish all ballots in advance, not their content, but a uuid associated to each of them, and whether it has been used or not. For each voter we mark a flag (voted/not voted). The number of voted ballots must match the number of voters who voted. New ballots cannot be created because they were made public in advance.

Comment 7 | created 2017-06-10T15:34:03Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307572240
In helios, if I delete the private key, can I still run the tally function and single out a single voter? If not, that may be a good compromise solution. Edit: I am not convinced... I may have to write that exploit to be sure. ;-)


Comment 8 | created 2017-06-10T15:46:06Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307572994
@mdipierro regarding your system: sure, though usually there are people who don't vote, so administrators can "ballot stuff" near the end of the election, right? Also, what prevents an election administrator from changing ballots?

Regarding Helios: if you delete the private key, then indeed the election administrator can no longer decrypt partial tallies as you suggested. But you can still do the complete election verification, since that depends only on the public keys. I think that's the solution you're looking for.

Comment 9 | created 2017-06-10T15:59:03Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307573743
No. Administrators cannot change votes or stuff ballots without being detected. The hash of  ballot is published (along with the uuid, before a vote is cast and after a vote is cast). The voter knows which one is its own ballot. The system does not record the link but the voter is told when he votes. He can check that his/her ballot is not tampered with. Administrators can stuff ballots but this would also be detected because either the number of voted ballots no longer matches the number of voters who voted, or the administrator would have to flag a voter who did not vote as a voter who did vote. That voter would know somebody voted on his behalf.

Regarding helios. I will look into your suggestion. I agree if that is the case, it improves the situation. Continuing to play my role of devil's advocate: An administrator could make a copy of that private key and when the database is published, use it to de-anonymize.

Comment 10 | created 2017-06-10T16:02:08Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307573962
@mdipierro I think if you're assuming administrators can copy secrets, then it's easy for administrators to keep a copy of which vote corresponds to which voter, too. I prefer a solution that keeps the link between voter and encrypted vote public, as that has many security/logging/auditing benefits, and then works the security around that :)

Comment 11 | created 2017-06-10T16:34:14Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307575893
yes and no. I can only talk about eVote because I know it best and perhaps some of its ideas can be implemented into Helios. In eVote each voter is emailed a uuid link. When the voter clicks on the clicks on a link a random ballot is assigned to the voter. The ballot also has a uuid and it is told to the voter. The voter uuid is used to authenticate the voter and flag it as "he voted" but the link between the voter uuid and the ballot uuid is not stored anywhere. This is designed to mimic the actual paper voting process: people show their ID to vote but then they get assigned a random booth. It is true that if an administrator could intercept all email communications, the administrator could tamper with the election. But this is true for Helios too. This is in my opinion an unsolvable problem. I wrote eVote based on requirements from the Python Software Foundation. At the time the requirements were that the code running on the system should never store enough information to allow de-anonymizing votes from any single snapshot of the database. We can assume nobody is tampering with the program while voting. The database can be made public at election closing.  In eVote we use public/private keys at the election level for the digital signatures for the ballots, because we do not want somebody else to contest an election based on a forged signature; but we do not store any secret of any kind that gives the administrator the power to decrypt something that voters would not be able to see themselves. Anyway.


Comment 12 | created 2017-06-10T16:51:04Z
Source: https://github.com/benadida/helios-server/issues/170#issuecomment-307576892

Ultimately, I'm sure different models can work.

The Helios model is one of universal verifiability, where each voter can verify their ballot was captured correctly, and anyone can verify that the tally is correct. There are two properties you want to consider: correctness of the tally, and privacy of the voters. With Helios, correctness is prioritized: there is no way for even one administrator to change the tally without being detected. Privacy is also important, though it is a slightly lower priority: if you have only one administrator, then technically that administrator *could* determine how you voted, but never change the outcome of the vote. If you're willing to have more than one administrator, you can get to a much higher level of privacy. Though it has never been proven to my knowledge, I believe there is an inherent tradeoff between correctness and privacy: I don't think you can have unconditional correctness and unconditional privacy. So Helios picks correctness and then does its best with privacy.

It's certainly possible you've solved this dilemma with eVote! That said, I would encourage you to publish your protocol and get it reviewed, because this stuff is very, very tricky, and Helios is the result of years of peer review by a number of experts. (Which doesn't mean Helios is perfect, just that we've worked through a lot of the core issues to some degree :)

Issue body:
After deleting the topic, the files remain on the server. If the topic has an image or file, it should also be deleted along with the topic (with the publication)

Files and images in the Upload folder on the server are not sorted by months or by date, in the future there will be a limit overflow ...

Also, the user cannot delete its own files from the server!
If the user or administrator deleted the publication from the forum irretrievably, then why store not used files on the server after removing the topic or publication?

Where is the logic ?

Comment 1 | created 2022-02-08T19:26:00Z
Source: https://github.com/NodeBB/NodeBB/issues/10144#issuecomment-1032979404
Files are not deleted from the server mostly because it is easier (note I didn't say _better_) to err on the side of caution and keep everything.

It is probably better to update this logic so that when a post is purged, its associated uploads are also deleted. An additional ACP option to preserve the files would be better in cases where storage is not a concern.

Secondly, re: the right to be forgotten (that is, deleting a user's own files on the server), the process to do this is to request account deletion from an admin. When an admin deletes your account, all of your content (topics, posts, uploads, etc.) are purged from the server.

_Re: sorting of files in the ACP, open a new issue for this._

Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
[Verify that users have a method to remove **or** export their data on demand.](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/4.0/en/0x16-V8-Data-Protection.md)

There are two requirements here:
* users must be able to export their data
* users must be able to remove their data

The way this requirement is currently stated allows implementors to choose either of these. I don't think that makes sense. Export and removal do not solve the same problem.

The "method" this requirements mentions can also be to email the support desk, it doesn't have to be integrated in the application, in my opinion. In that case, does this even belong in the ASVS? What is the application's role in this? Should every application have export functionality built in? Should every application have functionality to remove data built in?

Issue discussion:

Source: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/883#issuecomment-746614029

- Jim

Comment 3 | created 2021-03-13T12:36:01Z
Source: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/883#issuecomment-798299281
Just in case reminder (from Slack chat) that new requirements should be added to the end of (sub)category to keep current numbering as long as possible.

Comment 4 | created 2021-03-18T15:37:57Z
Source: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/883#issuecomment-802028449
The GDPR says users have a right to [receive](https://gdpr.eu/article-20-right-to-data-portability/) or [delete](https://gdpr.eu/article-17-right-to-be-forgotten/) their data. However, it doesn't say that this functionality should be present in the application. Technically, neither does the ASVS:

> Verify that users have a method to remove or export their data on demand.

Is it sufficient if I could call the help desk and a database administrator deletes some rows from the database? If so, does this belong in the ASVS? This seems to be more a business process verification than an application verification.

Comment 5 | created 2021-03-18T15:40:45Z
Source: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/883#issuecomment-802030570
The right to be forgotten is a core application need that relates to security and privacy. US laws are requiring this as well. Lets do it. But perhaps we need to make a special privacy option since this is only tangential to security?

Comment 6 | created 2021-03-18T16:47:37Z
Source: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/883#issuecomment-802102495
Till it's not required as functionality in application, this requirement or requirements, if we keep them, belong to V1.8.

edit: Actually those requirements makes sense and belong where they are.

We checked it from end-user perspective, and it is not clearly required to provide mentioned functionalities via user-interface.

But if user makes call to helpdesk (as an example), then in the application must be present a method or procedure to export and/or delete user-related data.

Issue body:
# Issue

We do have an interested in being alerted of users with the same IP as a banned player, which is why we have `logIps` true. However, it stores players IPs in `bm_player_history` indefinitely with no easy way of purging older entries (older than X days).

# Suggsetion
Add a `cleanUp` configuration for logged (but not necessarily banned) IP. If there already exists one then I'm sorry but I couldn't find it.

# Information
Our `bm_player_history` table has ~2,141,887 entries. :no_mouth: 
Current cleanUp options:
```yaml
# Keep records for number of days, use 0 to never delete
cleanUp:
  kicks: 30
  banRecords: 0
  ipBanRecords: 0
  ipMuteRecords: 0
  muteRecords: 0
  readWarnings: 0
  unreadWarnings: 0
```

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2018-04-25T20:53:51Z
Source: https://github.com/BanManagement/BanManager/issues/766#issuecomment-384430520
That would cover the history table, however, what about the `players` table (bm_players) which stores the last known IP? The issue with that is BM presumes a player always has an ip address on record. Would replacing that with `127.0.0.1` suffice? Or is that not necessary? The alternative of wiping the player from the table wouldn't be wise as it's required as a reference to past punishments.

As an aside, this doesn't necessarily have to be actioned by the plugin, you could set up a cron job deletes any old ip addresses or use MySQL's event scheduler.

Comment 2 | created 2018-04-25T21:45:43Z
Source: https://github.com/BanManagement/BanManager/issues/766#issuecomment-384444520
The primary interest of the `bm_players_history` table is mainly the vast amount of data it holds. We don't have a reason to store the IP-address of a player who joined on our servers 5 years ago and never again since. I didn't know `bm_players` also stored the IP-address of players, and it would also be of interest to clear that as well if it is too old. Is this table only for players with punishment-history of for everyone?

Would it be possible to wipe a player from the database if a configurable X amount of days have passed since they last logged in (by the bm_players lastSeen) - **and** - if they have **no** previous punishments? :thinking: 

> The right to be forgotten only applies if the personal data is no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; and/or there are no overriding legitimate grounds for processing.

The GDPR is only against storing information about **everyone, forever**. It is perfectly fine to store minimum required information to ensure system-operational capabilities (i.e in this case maintaining a ban system (list of IP's) ) as long as is required. :slightly_smiling_face:

Issue title: Need: UUID for the fingerpringt processor
Project: elastic/beats
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['pseudonymization']"
GitHub labels: ["enhancement", "Team:Services"]
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 3; discussants: 3
Reported: 2020-11-26 08:49:10+00; last active: 2022-03-31 08:26:54+00
Issue number: 22770

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 3/3
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
**Describe the enhancement:**
Introduction of the UUID method for the fingerprint processor

**Describe a specific use case for the enhancement or feature:**
I'm trying to demonstrate gdpr pseudonymization compliance using the filebeat as described in this article using Logstash: https://www.elastic.co/de/blog/gdpr-personal-data-pseudonymization-part-1
To make the pseudoids bulletproof, I need the UUID method, unfortunately the fingerprint method has no UUID method at the moment.
*UseCaes*
Data comes in. I would like to pseudonymize a certain field. Filebeat checks if the data has this field, if so create a new document in the Index Identities, create a mapping and replace the personal data with a pseudoId created by UUID in the Index Events.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2020-11-26T17:34:07Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/beats/issues/22770#issuecomment-734418811
Pinging @elastic/integrations-services (Team:Services)

Comment 2 | created 2020-12-03T20:15:06Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/beats/issues/22770#issuecomment-738281786
From logstash documentation about the UUID method: 

> When the target option is set to UUID the result won’t be a consistent hash but a random UUID. To generate UUIDs, prefer the uuid filter.

Using the fingerprint processor in Beats you can only hash. This gives you a value that depends on your event contents. Basically a stable hash. The UUID method generates a random value only (no hashing of fields is required). This is why one should better use the UUID filter.

In Beats there is a [add_id](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/beats/filebeat/current/add-id.html) processor. Currently it only supports the elasticsearch method, which is constructed based on the timestamp and some kind of counter, which speeds up indexing a little.

Skimming the article the Logstash fingerprint processor is used for consistent hashing (which the UUID method is not). The Logstash filter pipeline in the article first computes a consistent hash from the fields and finally uses the ruby filter to split the event into two events. The identity event has the form `{"_id": <consistent hash>, "<key>": <consistent hash>, "value": <value>}`. The way the pipeline is setup, there doesn't seem to be a lookup feedback cycle, meaning the consistent hash is a must. The strategy depends on Elasticsearch removing duplicate fields for already known hashes.

In order to replace the consistent hash with an UUID one might want to write the complete filter in ruby, as the filter would need to maintain a table of `concrete value => random ID`, in order to ensure that common values will match a single document in the identity index. What is nice about this approach is, that without the identity index one can not "attack" the hash trying to reconstruct the original entry from dictionaries. Drawback is that the table maybe needs to be "cleaned" from time to time and IDs might change between restarts unless you find a way to load your lookup table on start.

Without the table managed within the ruby filter, each event will produce an entry in the identity index otherwise. The advantage of having a common ID for matching values like "user" is, that it is still possible to correlate related events or product meaningful metrics via aggregations, without having the original values. Producing full randomized values per entry makes it impossible to correlate events for related (anonymized) entries without additional processing.

Currently processors in filebeats can not produce new events. There are technical limitations that currently make this impossible. AFAIK ingest node can't be used to split the event into two events as well. In this regard Logstash is most flexible right now.

Comment 3 | created 2022-03-31T08:26:53Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/beats/issues/22770#issuecomment-1084259146

Source: https://github.com/fgpv-vpgf/fgpv-vpgf/issues/2733#issuecomment-392085891
### Google Tag Manager
- Does not replace Google Analytics (GA), instead it is capable of watching for DOM changes and interactions and integrating these actions into reportable events for analytics (among other things).
- Not strictly needed, you can place GA code throughout your code base to send event information (like when a panel is opened, some feature is used, or a plugin is loaded. In some cases we may need to place GA code directly into RAMP
- The benefit is that most interactions do not need any modification to the RAMP code base. You can tell tag manager to watch for a certain element (CSS selector or ID) to be visible, clicks, javascript errors, scrolling etc). These changes are done in the tag management site, not in the code base.

### Google Analytics
Comprehensive tool which reports among others:
- Users country / region
- browser type and version
- time spent
- events triggered by tag manager
- event flow (order of actions they took on the page)
- abandonment analysis (why did they leave, what action did they take)
- performance benchmarks (page load, usability)
- compliance tools we can use (IP anonymization) so that no personal information is provided

### Next steps
1) Determine how we want to report events. We can set 4 event parameters (Category, Action, Label, and Value). This can be something along the lines of (UI, Panel, Grid-UI, Open) and (API, Plugin, Added, myPluginName) for example

2) Tag manager has versioning, so it can track variations of RAMP. Figure out how this will work with our versioning.

3) Determine things tag manager can't watch or would be difficult (perhaps plugins, API use) so that these events can be hard-coded into RAMP where needed.

4) If GA or tag manager is already present on the page, determine steps needed to add our tracking code, if not load appropriate google scripts.



Comment 6 | created 2018-05-28T12:51:59Z
Source: https://github.com/fgpv-vpgf/fgpv-vpgf/issues/2733#issuecomment-392519105
#### Overview

Google Tag Manager (GTM) is a script we insert on bootstrap that together with its web interface is capable of watching the DOM for triggers such as elements becoming visible, clicks, JS errors, scrolling and more. You can also set timers that run custom JS code which would be able to inspect the current API state. Custom events from within RAMP can be pushed when the triggers are more complex and would be too difficult to implement within the GTM interface. 

We only need to include the GTM code snippet in ramp. Any events captured by GTM will be passed to our Google analytics (GA) account which provides advanced analysis on the events, times, order of events etc. 

#### Treasury board compliance

We will anonymize IP addresses where GTM performs this anonymization before writing it to disk. We will limit stored records to 18 months per treasury board guidlines. No personal information is uploaded and therefore we meet all guidelines.  

#### Loading script

Google supports multiple GTM script tags to be used where there is more than one tracking account. So if the WET template contains GTM code, it is recommended to also include another GTM script code using our tracking ID. Ramp can insert this script on bootstrap.

#### Manual events (coded in RAMP)

GTM can handle most tags and events. In some cases we might need to manually send an event from RAMP to GTM, but I believe this is unlikely given the available options. If needed however, this is done by pushing an object to a global `dataLayer` object which is watched by the GTM. An example:

```js
dataLayer.push({
	event: "RV-UI",
	eventCategory: "Panels",
	eventAction: "Open",
	eventLabel: "Grid-UI"
});
```

Since there can be multiple instances of GTM on a page (WET, RAMP) and they must both use the same global `dataLayer` array, the solution is to use custom `event` properties like we did above with `RV-UI`. In GTM we can set a trigger for the event `RV-UI` and push that to our analytics account. Other instances of GTM would ignore these events.

#### Event reporting

We will have a few custom event types (subject to change/add/remove based on feedback):
- RV-UI : For UI interaction with panels, settings, menu etc.
- RV-API: To track general API use at a high level (API class creation) and common uses
- RV-PLUGINS: Capture loaded intentions/extension
- RV-ERROR: Capture specific points of failure or try to catch most/all RAMP errors to see general app health

#### Versioning

As different versions of RAMP are released, the trigger type/selector may change due to changes in our html or user flow. GTM has the concept of versioning, and assigning versions to environments. For example, if we change a buttons name/id that was being used by GTM to track clicks in ramp v2.4.0 then we could save the new name/id under v2.4.0 in GTM and update the script type GTM uses to point to version v2.4.0. v2.3.0 (with the old name/id) would continue to be tracked correctly as well since it is using the v2.3.0 version as it always has.

That's true, and it's fine if there is/isn't an existing gtm script. gtm supports/needs a separate script for each tracking account on a page. They must share a global `dataLayer` object, however pushed data to the global `dataLayer` must be configured within the gtm site for it to be recorded on analytics. If, for example, two tracking accounts exist on a page with two corresponding apps which listen on the same event name then either app can trigger both accounts listeners. This is avoided by using non-generic event names.

I thought about tracking multiple maps on a page, and it is possible. Before implementing something like this it might be worth reporting how many pages use multiple maps and if the number is large enough to go ahead with implementing it. 

The current PR segments analytics by ramp version, multiple maps could be another possible segment.

Issue body:
## Summary

For privacy reasons we'd love to use Amplitude without using any cookies nor local storage.

## Motivations

Due to the "Cookie Law" in Europe, a web site or page needs a "cookie approval" before storing anything in a cookie or in a local storage. However it's OK to still log, using amplitude, events and information relative to the website as long as everything stays in RAM. This could be used for the landing page to compute direct conversion even for users who don't approve the use of cookies or local storage.

In terms of implementation, I could provide a PR, if you're OK with the idea: the current implementation already works without using the storage, the storage is only useful when the page is refreshed.

For the moment the way we handle it is to use the `disableCookies` option and clear the local cache on the callback of every logEvent, however this is suboptimal as some data is still stored and could be kept if the user closes the page before Amplitude server's response. It's also suboptimal because we're basically undoing what the library does, so it would be cleaner not to do it in the first place.

Issue body:
First, I want to say that JUMP’s goal is to promote the safety of our riders while partnering with cities to provide access to the data required for city-planning.  As noted during the workshop, sharing raw location data in the form of start and stop locations, route data and/or trip history presents a risk of re-identification that may endanger the privacy of our users.  

Below, I have outlined a few approaches to lessening the privacy impact related to  trip data, some of which have already been mentioned in issues #68, #66 & #61.  JUMP would appreciate the opportunity to discuss any of these approaches in more detail with LADOT staff.

### Trip Data Obfuscation Methods

* Limit location & time accuracy:  limiting GPS precision based on population density of a particular city in combination with time aggregation is one means of anonymizing data.  Depending on LA’s population density and trip count, providing GPS with two or three decimal places and on an hourly time aggregation may be a acceptable solution.  One way to implement this within the MDS is to add an “accuracy” field in the collection of all timestamp and location data.

* Snap to nearest census block: operators can systematically fuzz the start and stop locations by “snapping” location data to the center of the nearest census block or predefined area.  To maintain privacy, route location data should also be anonymized across location and time. 
  
* Aggregate route data:  operators may provide specific route data only once a minimum number of trips using that route occured in a specific time period.  For example, route data would be provided for a trip from point A to point B only when at least 30 similar trips occured in a given time period.  Start and stop locations could also be anonymized by either “snapping” or limiting GPS accuracy. 

### GBFS Feed - Real Time Availability 

As designed, the GBFS feed does not adequately protect the privacy of its users.  While the bikes “on trip” are not shown, anyone with access to the system can easily reconstruct a trip by tracking when bikes are reserved (at which time they disappear from the map) and when the reservation ends (when they reappear). This information can be used to build a database of historic trip information and ultimately re-identify users based on their trip history.  One fix for this problem is to scramble the bike identifiers during a trip so it is impossible to determine which start and stops constitute a unique trip. 

### User Consent   

Operators may offer users the choice to share trip  data with cities without anonymization via opt-in.  This could be in addition to a truly anonymized method above, which would not be subject to consent.

Issue body:
Hello, 
I am using the latest telegram version and have my online status private (i.e. Last seen recently.), however when in groups, you can still see an estimate of when I was last online.

Example:
Let's say I was online 5 mins ago, user A was online 4 minutes ago and user B was online 6 minutes ago. On the group users list I will appear between those two users and with that you can see my exact status which is not very private.

Thank you.


Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2017-04-07T16:27:16Z
Source: https://github.com/telegramdesktop/tdesktop/issues/3230#issuecomment-292584073
@MiguelSOliveira You local online status is updated for users when you send a message there — you become online for about 30 seconds. That way the status may change inside group list. But otherwise the sorting is the same as the phrases used (last seen recently — about three days), the app doesn't "know the real status, but hides it" — this would be a privacy issue, the app really doesn't know those last seen times — so it can't show the right position in chat participants list anyway.

Comment 2 | created 2017-04-07T16:30:14Z
Source: https://github.com/telegramdesktop/tdesktop/issues/3230#issuecomment-292584900
The problem comes when a user that has this option deactivated (i.e. last seen status public). 
He sees something like:

User A - last seen 1 minute ago
Me - last seen recently
user B - last seen 3 minutes ago

Comment 3 | created 2017-04-07T16:32:47Z
Source: https://github.com/telegramdesktop/tdesktop/issues/3230#issuecomment-292585567
@MiguelSOliveira If you hide your last seen status from someone he doesn't have the exact last seen time in his app — no matter did he hide his last seen status from you or not. Only way this can happen is if he had your last seen status visible not too long ago (before you hide it) and uses that value or if his app saw some your action (like message was sent by you or typing was sent by you) and it updated your last seen status to that value.

Comment 4 | created 2017-04-07T16:37:03Z
Source: https://github.com/telegramdesktop/tdesktop/issues/3230#issuecomment-292586672

![ex](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8149533/24810344/08c5353e-1bba-11e7-816e-e4578f07607b.png)
I'm not saying he has the exact value. I'm saying he has an interval of my last seen status.
From the example I gave above, anyone can see that I was online between 1 to 3 minutes ago.

I'm saying someone with hidden status should always appear on the bottom of the users list, unless he is online.

I may be wrong and this is indeed how it is supposed to be like and in that case I stand corrected.

Comment 5 | created 2017-04-07T16:52:57Z

@MiguelSOliveira He doesn't see this interval unless he receives it somehow. He can receive it by two ways: (1) he received it before he was restricted to your last seen status. (2) he saw some your action, visible to him, that triggered that you're online, like a new message or a typing action.

Released issue metadata:
Issue title: Private Community should obscure login failure results
Project: vanilla/vanilla
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['personally identifiable information']"
GitHub labels: []

Supplemental evidence: partial | comments retrieved 0/0
Scope: Historical GitHub public event text retrieved from GH Archive via ClickHouse. This is not a current issue snapshot or proof of a complete discussion. Event coverage can omit edits, deletions and comments. Archived issue-body and comment versions must be interpreted within this stated scope. Linked development material is collected separately.

Issue body:
Vanilla is most often used as a public platform, where usernames are not considered personally-identifiable information (PII) and it's trivial to iterate over usernames via profile URL (as with most social media platforms). It's also possible to derive a "username list" by attempting logins and recording whether that password was incorrect or the user did not exist, per error message. We do this because it adds no additional security to attempt to obscure usernames at this step, and because obtuse error messages are really bad UX.

However, if the Private Community addon is enabled, it's reasonable for someone to expect that information like usernames are not leaking. Therefore, I propose that the Private Community setting also obscure the login error message to be generic between non-existent or wrong-password. This provides additional warm fuzzies to the folks using that setting without setting up lame errors for everyone else.

Issue title: TURN-TLS support
Project: nextcloud/spreed
Issue type: issue

GitHub labels: ["4. to release", "enhancement", "feature: WebRTC \ud83d\udea1"]
Status in release: closed

Issue number: 257

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 46/46
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
It seems you only support UDP and TCP. However there is another transport mechanism called TURN-TLS, which wraps the whole thing into another TLS layer. This should be the last fallback for ugly company firewalls or so, which do deep package inspection and block non-HTTPS traffic on port 443.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2017-03-26T18:43:35Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-289305371

Comment 2 | created 2017-05-23T15:01:10Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-303426421
Firefox appears to have [added support for this in v53.](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1056934)

Comment 3 | created 2018-07-30T11:29:07Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-408832332
@fancycode any idea what would need to be done on our end?
CoTurn seems to support it:
> TLS (per RFC 5766 and RFC 6062): TLS1.0/TLS1.1/TLS1.2; ECDHE is supported.

Comment 4 | created 2018-07-30T13:39:35Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-408866490
It *should* be enough to also return `turns:` urls here:
https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/blob/d69d88bcd42e5953d4a82eb78ba26a912d96f507/lib/Config.php#L69

Needs some testing though.

Comment 5 | created 2019-04-26T19:13:31Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-487169701
@fancycode @nickvergessen 
I just faced the TURNS TLS question as well. Many guides state to enable TLS support in coTURN settings (my own HowTo as well), but actually coTURN allows to access plain on "tls-listening-port" as well (and the other way round), so it's up to the client to request via `turn://` or `turns://` and the coTURN settings do not matter at all, besides TLS cert required of course.

So if spreed/talk accesses via `turn://` only, then setting up TLS in coTURN has absolutely no effect (for Nextcloud Talk). So I need to update my HowTo 🙈: https://help.nextcloud.com/t/howto-setup-nextcloud-talk-with-turn-server/30794

TURN is such an essential part of getting Nextcloud Talk working throughout NAT and that it is never accessed via TLS (TURNS) is important to know to not give users a wrong impression about the connection type. So I think it would be beneficial to have these infos (e.g. based on the HowTo) to a more prominent/official place. What do you think?

And of course if applying TURNS is really that easy, it would be perfect to have a toggle within Talk app settings.
_____________
Side note: https://github.com/coturn/coturn/issues/33
- Security benefit of TURNS is very limited (WebRTC encrypted anyway).
- But it allows passing firewalls that allow transport layer encrypted requests only.

Comment 6 | created 2020-06-10T08:50:04Z

Comment 42 | created 2020-12-23T23:24:33Z
Source: https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257#issuecomment-750555885
@luminous706: The secret is not sent over the wire. It's used to compute a one-way hash which is sent in its place. You don't need an encrypted connection to protect the secret as it can't be recreated from the hash.

Furthermore, the browsers use end-to-end encryption for the voice and video channels, so those are encrypted regardless of whether a TURN server is used or not. 

Adding encryption at the TURN layer double encrypts the traffic, which isn't generally necessary and usually just adds overhead.

The primary benefit to using TLS or DTLS for the TURN connection is to allow traversing firewalls that otherwise try to block WebRTC traffic. Many firewalls block all UDP traffic, for those you fall-back to using TCP. Others block all traffic except on a few well-known ports, for those you shift the TURN server to a well-known and allowed port, like 443[*]. Some advanced firewalls perform deep-packet-inspection to try to determine what kind data the traffic really is, regardless of the port. For those, you wrap the WebRTC traffic inside an encrypted tunnel, e.g. TLS or DTLS. A TLS connection on port 443 is basically indistinguishable from `https:` traffic (except by doing traffic analysis and taking an educated guess) so gets through most firewalls and web proxies.

You can use Nextcloud Talk as it is today without worrying about your TURN server being compromised or your conversations  listened to. This feature is used to make connections when operating on hostile networks that will otherwise block your connections completely, e.g. coffee shop WiFi, hotels, locked-down enterprise networks, etc.

[*] Sharing port 443 with a web server on the same IP address can be done, but is not easy, using TLS can help there too.

Linked pages and attachments are not fetched. Issue body: Related to ushahidi/platform#1774 ### Expected behaviour When location is regarded as PII in a deployment, map coordinates for the post should be obfuscated when provided from the API, so that no one can retrieve the exact locations. This may be a randomisation within or an assignation to the centroid of a reasonably big geoblock (e.g. in function of the maximum allowed zoom level setting as specified in #1774) ### Actual behaviour Currently the API provides the exact coordinates as stored along with the post. Issue discussion: Comment 1 | created 2017-06-08T12:43:20Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-307091666 PII is incredibly important to our end users and clients. I believe that this could be pivotal in the ability for many clients to adopt the platform. Comment 2 | created 2019-06-09T22:39:42Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-500251302 I think this should be covered by the anonymization and precision level features. Closing but tagging @tuxpiper to reopen if necessary Comment 3 | created 2019-06-12T10:33:27Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-501215918 Agreed :+1: Comment 4 | created 2019-06-12T13:44:06Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-501279572 The map precision level of 2 is at 10km. What would a precision of 4 be? 1? I can see this starting to hinder smaller geographic deployments where the different surveys are more important than the geographic scale. What algo is the randomizer based on? Is it a true random from a physical source (ie Cloudflare) or computer generated? A goal of the masking of PII would be to have control to scale the range of randomness based on the variance between sources of PII within the map. If 100 sources live within 1.5km, PII randomness can be assigned to a very tight range. If 10 sources are covered over 100km in range, you may need to have a very wide value set for randomization unless that would defeat the purpose of the map, in which case, one should not use a map for this type of data. Comment 5 | created 2019-06-17T19:54:17Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-502827009 Thanks for the input @ClearLakeHABMap Apparently a level of 4 would already be giving out a precision of around 100m ... which is well, quite precise in a personal scale, I think. The function is not a randomiser, because it was deemed important that points in the map would appear stable, and storing randomised coordinates separately seemed... inconvenient. The function pretty much just snaps the coordinates to the nearest intersection point in a grid, drawn accordingly to the precision level. I'm assuming the estimated precision that is shown in Settings > General is calculated assuming locations around the equator, but not quite sure. This is a pretty crude approach, better approaches (in the shape of issues and/or pull requests of implementations :) ) are more than welcome. I think you are right that this "one size fit all" approach may not work well for deployments that have scopes covering areas with mixed population densities.. such as a lot of counties, states, as well as any country or continent. Dynamic approaches to solve this sound appealing. I am guessing it's a desirable trait to have the markers in the map appear stable as the map gets reloaded, or more markers are added.... which may make dynamic implementations harder. But curious what other people think about this. Comment 6 | created 2019-07-09T12:27:09Z Source: https://github.com/ushahidi/platform/issues/1775#issuecomment-509621574 @ClearLakeHABMap Hi there, I'd really like to understand more about your needs for a feature like this so i can better understand how to design the UX/UI. If you have a chance to email/message me that'd be amazing. eriol@ushahidi.com If not I've assigned this to go in my backlog of issues to improve from a UX pov.

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 3/3
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
## Type of issue
Feature request

## Description
CA government officials have indicated GPC should be treated as peer with USP string https://twitter.com/AGBecerra/status/1354850321692934144 .  We'd like to allow publishers to do a setConfig to read from the GPC api and change us privacy strings that consentmanagementusp.js passes to core from 1YYY (or 1---) to 1YNY when the GPC api is more conservative than the existing setting. 

We imagine the workflow would be publishers would set this config everywhere, nowhere, or only when CCPA or similar legislation applies according to their own perogative and if the third option, they would remain responsible for detecting if it applies. 

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2021-02-17T22:27:39Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/6270#issuecomment-780896180
Spoke with a couple of different privacy lawyers on this. The advice we received is to just pass the GPC HTTP header through the system and let bidders deal with it for now. I've also reached out to the IAB to get their take.

When CA writes a law linking CCPA and GPC more formal than a tweet, hopefully the IAB will react quickly and we'll follow their lead.

So for now, nothing to do on Prebid.js. I've opened https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/1712 to track the Prebid Server update. Once the issue of jurisdiction is more clear, we'll update this and PBS may tie the header to US Privacy or perhaps treat it like LMT.

Comment 2 | created 2021-02-17T23:30:23Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/6270#issuecomment-780922683
It seems like it makes the most sense to have the us-privacy string as the canonical value, and check GPC in one place only, then write us-privacy as appropriate given the GPC value. The publisher can do this, since they already have to set us-privacy when the "Do Not Sell" link on the page is clicked.

Comment 3 | created 2021-03-29T15:50:16Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/6270#issuecomment-809491357
@dmarti closing, thanks so much

Issue body:
Auto-prune inactive user accounts after a period of inactivity. The journal should be able to specify the period of inactivity, and the account into which the user should be merged. For example: if the journal enables this option, and sets the period of inactivity to 1 year, any user that hasn't logged in for 1 year should be merged into an admin account. 

This should be an option for journals, set by default to "off", and similar to the auto-pruning of registered but not verified accounts (see "require_validation" and "validation_timeout" in config.inc.php).

Comment 1 | created 2018-04-10T19:51:01Z
Source: https://github.com/pkp/pkp-lib/issues/3577#issuecomment-380225440
I can think of other useful conditions that would need to be met: they should have no submissions assigned, no discussions/notes, no review assignments, etc. -- basically no participation anywhere in the workflow.

Is the goal to help clean up spam registrations? Are we getting spam registrations en masse with the current releases of OJS, or is this an archaeological dig?

Issue body:
Many regulations, including Swedish Healthcare, require a minimum of 5 years log retention. 

We determined that offering long-term logs at the platform level runs the risk of GDPR non-compliance. Since logs contain personal data, retention schemes need to be carefully designed together with application-specific recovery processes. Specifically, the design needs to ensure erased personal data ([Art. 17 GDPR Right to erasure (‘right to be forgotten’)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/)) is not accidentally restored.

**Acceptance criteria**

* There is a public doc page with prose and copy-paste-able code snippets explaining how to set up long-term logs on top of Compliant Kubernetes.

**Non-goals**

* Please do not focus on backups as part of these issue. Swedish Healthcare regulations leave the question of retention for backups to be determined by the organization based on a risk analysis.

Issue body:
Screenshots with privacy by default, please - you will need to provide that in the EU because of the GDPR anyway.

How to fix it
* Screenshots without a network connection.
* Screenshot editing without a network connection.
* Save the screenshot locally by default.
* Suggest online saving services - opt-in.
* Remove all cached information about the screenshot after saving.


Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2017-11-28T16:39:17Z
Source: https://github.com/mozilla-services/screenshots/issues/3797#issuecomment-347583524
Elvin will comment on this one

Comment 2 | created 2018-01-09T17:07:26Z
Source: https://github.com/mozilla-services/screenshots/issues/3797#issuecomment-356349097
Thanks for the comment.  We strive for a product that respects privacy, from routing analytics pings through our servers to using randomly generated URLs instead of actual image URLs in them when we do collect URLs.  Breaking down your comment:

>     Screenshots without a network connection.
You already can if you click the download button.

>     Screenshot editing without a network connection.
Editing (annotations) hasn't officially launched yet, but we're working on it.  I think all of these tools live on the website, so they won't be available offline though.

>     Save the screenshot locally by default.
There is no default, you have to choose an option each time.  So, same as your first bullet point, click the download button and it works fine.

>     Suggest online saving services - opt-in.
We don't support any other services other than our own server right now.  If you don't click the 'save' button the image doesn't get sent to them.

>     Remove all cached information about the screenshot after saving.
Is there specific information you're thinking about?  I don't think we save any.

For those of you interested in already being able to provide a local phantomjs binary in the docker image, just add this to the dockerfile before setting of the default ENV variables (copied from https://github.com/wernight/docker-phantomjs/blob/master/Dockerfile):

```
# Install runtime dependencies
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        ca-certificates \
        bzip2 \
        libfontconfig 

RUN set -x  \
    # Install official PhantomJS release
 && apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        curl \
 && mkdir /tmp/phantomjs \
 && curl -L https://bitbucket.org/ariya/phantomjs/downloads/phantomjs-2.1.1-linux-x86_64.tar.bz2 \
        | tar -xj --strip-components=1 -C /tmp/phantomjs \
 && mv /tmp/phantomjs/bin/phantomjs /usr/local/bin
```

Dear indy team, even though this not an issue, I want to ask if you have investigated your mechanisms according to GDPR. It wood be very helpful for any application with users in the EU considering to integrate indy.

Thanks! 

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2018-02-21T17:48:55Z
Source: https://github.com/hyperledger-indy/indy-sdk/issues/539#issuecomment-367411139
This has been a subject of a lot of discussion in the Identity WG and other places.  Marta Piekarska is leading a collaborative effort to build out a paper on how Blockchains in general can address GDPR requirements here:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wnRYOZrGZS6h_-PnJRaq1pAc35GrfGUZcXh46sTHdFQ/edit#heading=h.xlkpssu5kfbq

Certainly we think that Indy's approach has many advantages when it comes to giving a user the ability to manage data sharing and meet GDPR requirements, but I am not aware of a paper that specifically addresses how Indy or an instance of Indy like Sovrin addresses GDPR requirements, but I could see how we could build out something very useful, and it would be a welcome contribution.

Comment 2 | created 2018-03-06T10:48:37Z
Source: https://github.com/hyperledger-indy/indy-sdk/issues/539#issuecomment-370741605
I wrote an article about the greatest challenge, Right to Erasure: https://journal.tiiqu.com/open-questions-about-gdpr-compliance-in-the-context-of-blockchain-technologies-55f51860b048

While many properties of blockchain are great, this one is the most difficult to solve. It means that no personal data can be uploaded to the chain itself, only verifiers of personal data. The best way to link the verifier to the personal data would be ZKPs, simple hashes are considered pseudonymization, not anonymization, even though this opinion is questionable from a technical point of view (it is equivalent to say that good hashing can be backlinked or well encrypted data isn't private, the hacking procedures are  the same...).

So if you implement ZKPs as verifiers on the legder for personal offchain identity data, then you will be in a great position:-)

Comment 3 | created 2018-09-19T19:48:13Z
Source: https://github.com/hyperledger-indy/indy-sdk/issues/539#issuecomment-422934839
We are using Jira to track issues now, please use this [Jira IS-996 ticket](https://jira.hyperledger.org/browse/IS-996) for any further discussion.
