Issue number: 1327

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 0/0
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
This is a follow up to #1287. We came up with the idea of scrambling evaluation results as a part of the anonymization. Quote from @janno42:

"then @karyon and i discussed that it is better to randomize answers because there might be the following case: users who have access to production might find unpublished courses in the anonymized data and can find results there based on answer distribution of other courses and de-anonymizing contributor's names. this is a very special case and there wouldn't be much data available as a course is only then not published if less than two participants voted for it - but nevertheless there might be data leaked.
so we decided that answer counters should be set randomly on anonymization. the answer count per question should (roughly) stay the same during the process and it must be made sure that the answer count never exceeds the number of voters in the course."

We had two implementations flying around in that debate:
- One summed up the answer count, iterated over the RatingAnswerCounters and then took a random number between 0 and the remaining answers and assigned it to the current counter. This can be found [here](https://github.com/fsr-de/EvaP/pull/1287/commits/2c20342a61409f560aeea93a0d77e2bec9a5ee42#diff-8966c64d41a29b22e8ee43d34675dc33R220) but is biased towards giving higher vote counts to the answer counters we are looking at earlier
- The other one was given [here](https://github.com/fsr-de/EvaP/pull/1287#pullrequestreview-218545677). Basically, give every counter a random number between 0 and the count of votes, then divide by a factor so that the vote count matches the earlier result again. In order to keep the count of votes equal, one would have to then distribute the error evenly to the counters. This will give more uniform results but has more clean up to do.

Issue discussion:
[No issue comments at retrieval time.]
categories: 去标识、最小化与再识别
治理、责任与需求权衡
results.rationale: #1287 的后续：在匿名化时打乱评教结果。动机是拥有生产权限者可能在匿名化数据里识别未发布课程（少于两名参与者投票才不发布），并借其他课程的答案分布反推，从而去匿名化贡献者姓名；因此决定匿名化时随机化答案计数，同时要求每题答案总数大致不变，且任何一项计数不得超过该课程投票人数。讨论给出两版实现：一是先汇总答案总数，再按 RatingAnswerCounters 逐个取 0 到剩余数的随机值分配，实现简单但对靠前的计数项系统性偏高；二是先给每项一个 0..票数的随机数，再按因子缩放回原总数并均匀分摊误差，分布更均匀但需额外清理。正文无评论，无实现或合并证据。

Issue body:
- [X] I have searched open and closed issues for duplicates

----------------------------------------

### Bug description
The Signal Desktop debug log reveals the last three digits of a contact's phone number, not just the last two as described in https://github.com/WhisperSystems/Signal-Android/wiki/Submitting-useful-bug-reports#debug-log-privacy. (As of now the Signal Desktop wiki is empty so I can't point to that instead.)

### Steps to reproduce
- Open Signal Desktop
- Click three dots at middle top
- Click "Submit debug log"
- Look at log

**Actual result:** Log entries with three digits revealed, like:
$TIMESTAMP PUT https://textsecure-service-ca.whispersystems.org:80/v1/messages/+[REDACTED]123

**Expected result:** Log entries with only two digits revealed, like:
$TIMESTAMP PUT https://textsecure-service-ca.whispersystems.org:80/v1/messages/+[REDACTED]23

### Platform info
**Operating System**: Ubuntu 16.04.2 running Unity
**Browser**: Chrome 56.0.2924.87
<!-- you can see Signal's version number in your browser's extensions page: chrome://extensions -->
**Signal version:** 0.30.0

### Extra note
I noticed this because I saw another completely unrelated issue that looked sort of like mine, and the issue creator was asked to submit a debug log. I went to look for my own debug log out of curiosity and was concerned that the UI said the log would be posted publicly but not where. It also says I may examine and edit before submitting, and I first thought this meant that if I clicked submit I would be taken to another page or screen where I could edit the log. After further examination (without submitting any debug log) I understood that the message meant I should edit the log in the box I was already looking at before clicking "Submit". Then I wondered about personally-identifiable information and found the two digit message in the Signal Android wiki and then found it was actually three for Desktop. (I do see only two digits revealed in the debug log on an Android device.) I'm still not totally sure where the logs go, but looking at other issues, I think they become anonymous secret gists.

I think the two-vs-three digit discrepancy is a bug -- in documentation if nothing else -- but all of this together makes submitting debug logs feel pretty scary to me. I would advise anyone I know, especially less technical people, to stay away from the submit debug log UI unless they feel confident enough to carefully review and scrub it for themselves.

(Great product and service by the way! I hope you receive this issue as constructive criticism.)

categories: 同意、拒绝、撤回与偏好执行
隐私控制可用性与系统兼容
results.rationale: IE 的高级隐私设置设为阻止第一方 Cookie、仅允许会话 Cookie 时，Sails 0.12.3 + connect-mongo 每次请求都新建 session id，导致 CSRF mismatch 等故障。维护者解释 IE 所谓 session cookie 实为零或过去 TTL 的 cookie，与 sails.sid（实为认证 cookie）语义不同，因此需对该类 UA 把会话 cookie 的 expires 设为 false 使其成为 transient cookie，并建议放在 hook 里对每个请求生效。报告者指出若全局这样设置，普通 IE 用户关浏览器就丢购物车，于是改为先设置一个探测 cookie 检查该设置是否被接受，只对被限制的 IE 使用 transient cookie，其余 IE 恢复 30 天有效期。最终属用户侧 hook 方案自测可用，未见上游内建或提交。
results.scope_note: 用户 hook 方案验证可用；未上游内建

Issue body:
## What is the problem we are solving 
GDPR and other European local regulations force all European websites to:
- inform visitors / users if you collect personal data and what you do with them.
- request consent from the visitor / users to do so for each type of cookie.

We shouldn't collect and use non-compulsory data through cookies without the explicit consent (default opt-in doesn't work anymore) 
Today we don't ask any consent and collect and use data through cookies without our users knowing about it.
The only cookie I saw through Ghostary is New Relic which I guess is compulsory for the service we give (what it is used for again?) but maybe there are others.
Also some instances use Google Analytics, if so there are new trackers from Google that collect data.

## Success factors = expected outcome 
When a visitor connect for the first time to a local OFN instance, if the instance has toggled on the cookie banner agreement display, they should see the banner and be able to accept all cookies, set up more specifically which cookies they accept, or ignore (in that case all optional cookies should be deactivated by default) 
When they visit again they should always be able to change their cookies setting and opt-in our out.

## Metric
- All new visitor who have neither accepted cookies nor closed the banner should see it when they connect to the local instance URL.
- If a cookie is disabled the users data are not collected.
- If a cookie is enabled the users data are collected and can be used for the specified service.

## Useful information for/from inception
A spike has been done by Maikel on which cookies we use: https://github.com/openfoodfoundation/openfoodnetwork/issues/2240
That has enabed Myriam to build a UX proposal based on previous investigations about the law and some examples that seems aligned with the law.
https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1uMWiW6lQhqexAe_uFmjp5QNAM1zLfnIe1bF3-_Nb5xo/edit?usp=sharing

## Link to the "Icebox" item in Discourse
https://community.openfoodnetwork.org/t/users-know-clearly-which-cookies-are-used-and-can-refuse-them/1252

## First feature candidate to be implemented
Based on first tech inception by Maikel: Implement a toggle on-off banner (instance level) that enable  user to accept all cookies or view cookie policy and settings, in that case the only cookie they can be enabled/disabled is google analytics (if instance uses it).

As a result, the customer will see an invoice from another customer. This is a big problem from a privacy point of view. Please urgently for a solution! The problem occurs in the Order.php at the function setLastInvoiceNumber, because there the last number is queried and then +1 is added. With two simultaneous queries it happens that the same number is assigned twice. `if ($number) { $sql .= (int) $number; } else { $getNumberSql = '(SELECT new_number FROM (SELECT (MAX(`number`) + 1) AS new_number FROM `' . _DB_PREFIX_ . Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
We've been getting a lot of removal requests lately, and it seems worth it to take a slightly less open approach to publishing. 

Current proposals for removal from public search are:

1. Non-precedential cases. This currently is about 500,000 cases.
2. Cases from certain jurisdictions or courts that are more likely to have sensitive cases.
3. Any case mentioning certain words (like "asylum", for example)

We can make these rules as complex as we can dream up, but the idea here is to strike a better line between "publish everything in the name of openness" and "people have legit privacy rights". 

For example, looking at the above, I don't see a lot of benefit to publishing non-precedential cases — they're likely to be small-time, nobody is likely to look directly for them, and the people that these pages do attract to CourtListener probably didn't want to land there anyway. OTOH, some of the people in these cases are legitimately bad people, like fraudulent accountants and child molesters. OTOH again, some of these people are trying to move on with their lives and have served their time. Are we more moral to hide these or to show them? It's not altogether clear.

Currently, we only hide cases that:

1. Have a social security number (which we also X-out), or
2. Have an alien ID number, or
3. Emailed to have their case blocked.

There are currently about 2000 cases that we've blocked through manual or automated means.

I'd be very interested in a discussion of how we might improve our approach to this problem.

Comment 7 | created 2017-05-31T18:05:57Z
Source: https://github.com/freelawproject/courtlistener/issues/691#issuecomment-305269724
There is value in all of the following:
 - people's privacy, regardless of if it is recognized via formal methods like the European right to be forgotten or not
 - public records being made available
 - CourtListner being found in search results, so that it can be discovered as a resource
 - Not hiding any resources from CourtListener APIs

It looks like there are at least three methods by which a resource could be prevented from showing up in search results:
 - someone makes a request of the search engine, which is out of our hands
 - someone makes a direct request of CourtListener, which is covered by https://www.courtlistener.com/terms/#removal
 - CourtListener proactively hides a resource from search engines as mentioned in the first message in this issue

Resources include:
 - opinions
   -  precedential and non-precedential
   - by case type
   - by court
   - by data in the documents like Social Security Number mentioned in the first message in this issue
 - RECAP archives, some of which may contain sensitive information that is missed by the OCR process due to being handwritten
 - Oral arguments, with the expectation that at some point Google will allow audio search
 - Judges - should these ever be hidden?
 - Visualizations - someone could request that either one they authored or one that mentions them be hidden

It appears that any actions by search engines are out of our control. We can respond to any request for removal short of a crawler requesting that all resources be removed. It is the last category or preemptive hiding that is the curious one.

I like the idea of keeping track of how many resources are not exposed to search engines and reporting that under "The Numbers". This serves the purpose of both disclosing to the public at large, without outing the particular resources that are hidden, and reminding us of what portion of our resources we are choosing to hide.

I think @Colinstarger makes a good case for keeping non-precedential cases unhidden.

I could see some family court, bankruptcy, asylum and other case types being considered for blanket hiding. I do think our policy need to be explicit about these decisions.

In that someone could use RECAP and make records more public than the court makes them (by removing the paywall and exposing their content to search engines) I'm leaning toward rules that hide portions of those resources automatically. This could be based on keywords or if the metadata supports it case types.

I'm less concerned at the moment about the audio of oral arguments, but that could just be because I'm not aware of what Google is capable of in that area.

I'm leaning toward keeping the Judge profiles as unhidden as possible.

I'd default to keeping visualizations unhidden unless a request was received.

Comment 8 | created 2017-05-31T18:47:48Z
Source: https://github.com/freelawproject/courtlistener/issues/691#issuecomment-305281219
PlainSite offers similar functionality to CourtListener, and we receive around ten takedown requests a day. It's admittedly quite difficult to handle them all, and it offers a sense of what it must be like to be an actual judge, constantly on the receiving end of a request firehose.

We think it's actually important to have multiple, competing legal research services precisely because different services will have different approaches not just to functionality, but also to the availability of data. Our Privacy Policy ([https://www.plainsite.org/legal/privacy.html](https://www.plainsite.org/legal/privacy.html)) spells out exactly how we handle requests. The one line summary is that we are strongly biased in favor of transparency and against any form of censorship (de-indexing, deletion, etc.), unless we see a valid court order, because:

1. That approach is the only approach consistent with court precedent. Every takedown response we decline includes the following text (with links that don't carry over here): "There is a presumption of public access to court records and you have not identified a compelling privacy interest. "'Historically, courts have recognized a ‘general right to inspect and copy public records and documents, including judicial records and documents.’' Kamakana v. City & County of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Nixon v. Warner Communications, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978)). 'This right is justified by the interest of citizens in ‘keep[ing] a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies.’' Id. (quoting Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598). Access to judicial records, however, is not absolute. Id. A party seeking to seal a pleading or a dispositive motion (as well as any attached exhibits) must show that there are 'compelling reasons' to do so and that outweigh the public's interest in disclosure." See also Doe v. Lee, Docket No. 23, and Eng v. Pacermonitor.com et al."
2. We aren't judges, elected or appointed. If the courts have put something in the public domain, we treat it as such.
3. We and our principals have been in court before, repeatedly, against powerful defendants. There is always an incentive for the powerful and corrupt to hide information, and they are **well aware** of that incentive. When information cannot be obtained, fraud thrives. _See_ "Donald Trump".
4. Our experience handling takedown requests for five years suggests that the ones who shout the loudest and most viciously about being harmed are, without exception, the most dangerous individuals who merit the most transparency. Note the remarkable overlap in our tag for "Individuals Who Have Threatened PlainSite" (https://www.plainsite.org/tags/individuals-who-have-threatened-plainsite/) and robots.txt for Justia (https://dockets.justia.com/robots.txt).

One important difference, to the best of my knowledge, between our handling of takedown requests and CourtListener's is that our system is now almost completely automated. We get the odd request that requires a custom e-mail response, but most fit into our pre-determined categories for approval or declination. This greatly enhances request clarity, efficiency and [non-]customer satisfaction.

As for what to leave and what to de-index, it's not really our place to tell our competitors how to do business or run their non-profits. But that's how we run ours, and we run ours in accordance with principles that we believe are best for the country and the courts overall.

I run [Docket Alarm](https://www.docketalarm.com/), which faces similar issues as other organizations here. We are upfront about our removal policy on our [removal page](https://www.docketalarm.com/Remove). 

I agree with @PlainSite that we are not judges. However, Docket Alarm comes to the opposite conclusion: we assume that if someone asks to suppress a page, it may be causing them harm, and unless we see an obvious public interest in the availability of the case, we suppress the page from search engine results.

We strive to automatically suppress from search engines the categories listed on our removal page using a variety of automated means. Further, we automatically suppress cases from search engines that contain keywords that suggest privacy interests may be at issue (e.g., "divorce", "children", "minor", etc.).

Some other pragmatic issues to consider:
1. Aggressively publishing sensitive material (even if legal) may hurt efforts to open up court records, which in turn will have a negative impact on our larger and longer term goal to make legal information accessible.
2. Being responsible stewards of sensitive material (even if public) raises the credibility of each of our organizations individually, as well as our industry group as a whole. 
3. Many take-down requests come from people who were not involved in a lawsuit, but have the same name as someone else who was. We should strive to eliminate confusion and any collateral damage caused by a strict open access policy.
4. Many take-down requests come from people with limited monetary means, and we should not disproportionately harm those that are less able to protect themselves.
5. Many take-down requests come from people with limited technical means. The take-down process should be easy-to-use so that those with limited technical abilities are not disproportionately harmed because they are unable to use an interface.
6. The EU's "right to be forgotten", COPA, and some state laws potentially raise legal issues. Being a responsible legal steward of legal information will reduce potential risk to each of our organizations individually, and to our group as a whole.
7. Under no foreseeable circumstances should we impose a fee on users to suppress material. While I'm sure someone could make a buck, it's immoral and we should condemn this behavior.
8. While we suppress certain pages from search engines, paying users see all. The goal is to avoid causing harm as a result of informal Google searches, not to eliminate the record altogether.

In short, our mission should be a positive one on society, which responsibly considers and balances the benefits and harms of making court material readily accessible. We need to make clear that we take this responsibility seriously. Docket Alarm is happy to cooperate with the other organizations here to present a joint policy.

Wow. I'm glad so many people have contributed to this conversation. As a recovering philosopher, my inclination is to have long discussions on the most arcane subjects imaginable, but in this instance I'm less inclined to engage on all the good points being made because I'm compelled in this case by very mundane practical considerations. That is:

1) I have long wanted us to automate this process. If that's what @mlissner intends to do as a result of this discussion, then I'm open to a much wider range of solutions.
2) However, I have the impression that he instead intends to simply automatically de-index from search engines some subset of the corpus in an attempt to bring the request volume down and to continue to handle the remainder manually. Mike's time is better spent on almost anything else other than manually responding to these, so I want to minimize that effort. Consequently, I'd favor de-indexing automatically:

- All "unpublished" cases. (This is the main thing that helps with volume).
- The specialized military courts (United States Air Force Court of Criminal Appeals, Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, Army Court of Criminal Appeals, United States Court of Military Commission Review, Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals,
United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, Board of Veterans' Appeals)
- U.S. Tax Court and all state-level tax courts
- Merit Systems Protection Board	
- All Bankruptcy Court documents (from dockets < n entries) and all documents from district court level bankruptcy courts
- All Workers Compensation Commissions, Industrial Claim Appeals Offices, Compensation Review Boards, or Departments of Industrial Accidents
- All Family courts and Surrogate courts
- All State Bar Commissions (or decisions generally on lawyer discipline, wherever found)
- DHS/AAO/INS Decisions (that we don't currently even collect) but not federal circuit court level asylum decisions.

I want people to be able to find CL in search engines, but excluding these still leaves millions of search result entries in search and would, I hope, reduce the manual workload responding to these requests. Mike said all non-scotus asylum, but I think maybe the Circuit court level ones are too valuable a resource. 

If one day we had better subject-matter tagging of cases, we could consider a non-jurisdictional approach (all employment cases at the trial court level, for example), but until then we have to take a more blunt approach in order to move on to more important tasks.

Comment 15 | created 2017-06-05T19:17:15Z
Source: https://github.com/freelawproject/courtlistener/issues/691#issuecomment-306276604
My two cents: the above approach is overly broad.

- If a billionaire hedge fund manager or prominent attorney gets divorced and that fact is merely mentioned in a dispute over the business interests--suppressed. (https://www.plainsite.org/dockets/kfmizp0c/new-york-southern-district-court/usa-v-dreier/)
- If a billionaire hedge fund manager has a "minor" interest in a publicly-traded corporation that is the subject of a class-action lawsuit--suppressed. (https://www.plainsite.org/dockets/download.html?id=243914482&z=81fa365c)
- If a non-precedential opinion reveals a pattern of wrongdoing by a particular business interest or government agency--suppressed.
- If an MSPB case reveals wrongdoing by the VA, a federal government agency, or specific officials (Docket No. CH1221010192-B-1, Dr. Bennett S. Greenspan, then 464 F.3d 1297)--suppressed.
- If the President of the United States has declared bankruptcy four times, the initial filings and rulings are--suppressed.
- If a lawyer has been disciplined by the State Bar Court--suppressed.
- If a whistleblower such as Chelsea Manning is mistreated by a military tribunal--suppressed.

This goes to CourtListener's core purpose. If it's to only make readily available (e.g. Google, Bing, etc.) the least controversial cases that offend the fewest number of people, you might want to re-evaluate that aim. Obviously I'm not suggesting the opposite, that transparency sites should seek to offend. There has to be a balance. But balance takes a lot of work, not just keywords.

PlainSite definitely would not adopt or participate in any coordinated policy such as the one described above.

"minor AND child" in that same set of lower-level state courts (after 1967) yields 8,243 opinions today.

Comment 18 | created 2017-06-22T05:50:12Z
Source: https://github.com/freelawproject/courtlistener/issues/691#issuecomment-310282382
OK, final proposal that I think I'm going to move forward with, at least for the time being. We block the union of:

1. Everything containing "divorce" in a lower state court in the last 30 years ([45k cases][divorce]); AND
1. Everything containing "minor" and "child" in a lower state court in the last 30 years ([54k cases][minor]); AND
1. Everything containing "asylum" in federal district courts in the last 30 years ([1k cases][asylum]); AND
1. Everything containing "grams of cocaine" or "grams of crack cocaine" or "grams of marijuana" in any non-appellate court (state or federal) in the last 30 years ([10k cases][drugs])
1. Everything that's non-precedential in the last 30 years ([537k cases][nonp]); AND
1. Everything in the last 30 years in these courts, as listed by @brianwc ([52k cases][courts], [36k are bankruptcy][bankr]):

    - The specialized military courts (United States Air Force Court of Criminal Appeals, Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, Army Court of Criminal Appeals, United States Court of Military Commission Review, Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals,
    United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, Board of Veterans' Appeals)
    - U.S. Tax Court and all state-level tax courts
    - Merit Systems Protection Board	
    - All district court-level bankruptcy opinions
    - All Workers Compensation Commissions, Industrial Claim Appeals Offices, Compensation Review Boards, or Departments of Industrial Accidents

(30 years seems to be enough to satisfy the vast majority of the block requests we've gotten so far.)

Rules 1-4 are about 120k cases and help minors, asylum seekers, victims of the drug war, and divorcées. I'm pretty OK with these just coming out of Google, though I worry a bit about the drug war rule, that we'll be aiding some pretty bad people.

Rule 5 is a big one, over half a million cases, but the court said these weren't relevant, and we hide them from our own results by default, so I guess I'm OK with these being hidden from Google too.

Rule 6 I don't have a strong opinion on because I mostly don't know what goes down in those courts. I'll defer to @brianwc as a result. I'm a bit hesitant to pull down so much bankruptcy content though. A fair bit of this is probably corporate bankruptcies...do we really want to hide those too? Could we use [bankruptcy filing chapters][chapters] to refine this?

I found a bug in the plugin. When you setup "WP Job Manager" and set "Hide filled positions" and "Hide content within expired listings" the positions are still displayed in the WordPress native search.

I expected filled and expired position to be hidden from normal WordPress search. When the setup says so.

When searching I found that all of the expired and filled positions are displayed int the native search of WordPress.

#### Steps to Reproduce the Bug
1. Install Wordpress
2. Install WP Job Manager
3. Setup WP Job Manager (enable: "Hide filled positions" and "Hide content within expired listings")
4. Create 2 Jobs
5. Expire that job first one and mark the second one as filled
6. Do search with WordPress own search function using the name of the expired job or the filled job
7. Now the expired/filled position should be displayed in the search results

Issue title: Patient archiving
Project: DARIAEngineering/dcaf_case_management
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['anonymization', 'personally identifiable information']"
GitHub labels: ["backend"]
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 19; discussants: 5

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 19/19
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
Time to make an issue for this. Here is the issue: 

* There are some patient records who we are functionally done with; either people who have elected to carry their pregnancies, or who have had their procedures with assistance from us, or who have just timed out past the point where they need our help (120 days or so).
* We no longer really need a lot of their personally identifiable information (phone, name, etc) after this point.
* We also may need to create another entry for them if they seek our services again in the future, which conflicts with our validation on unique phone. (Right now we have a hacky workaround of setting a clearly fake phone number.)
* Thus, we need a way to 'archive' a patient to strip their information and get them out of rotation except for reporting. 

I think what this looks like from a technical perspective is wiping the phone numbers, setting an archive flag, and changing the name to a hash. A few caveats:

* People with the same phone number and name should have the same hash, so we can still identify people who are second people;
* Archiving should be irreversible.

Source: https://github.com/DARIAEngineering/dcaf_case_management/issues/812#issuecomment-275570670

https://github.com/colinxfleming/dcaf_case_management/wiki/Anonymization-notes

Source: https://github.com/DARIAEngineering/dcaf_case_management/issues/812#issuecomment-294631956

* Let's throw code relating to this in a `patient_archiving_helper` or `patient_archiving_concern` and include that in the patient model
* Probably the sum result of this should be something like `@patient.archive!` that does everything we need it to

Source: https://github.com/DARIAEngineering/dcaf_case_management/issues/812#issuecomment-294639970

Create fields for "changed appointment date", "changed clinic location", those but after the pledge is sent? etc?

Love the idea of an 'archive' field blacklist to deal with nuking sensitive fields.

Yas! First pass notes summing up the conversation so far and my thoughts and questions.

PRIMARY: Patients who are 120 days + past the [DATE] should be archived

  -  Needs:
     - patient privacy - remove no longer needed PII 
     - system limitation - phone number based ID conflicts
     - process is irreversible
  -  Wants
     - same patients archive linked somehow? (is this a need?)
     - use a concern `patient_archiving_concern`
     - invoke via `@patient.archive!`
  - Approach
     - Archive flag: on
     - Convert PII to non-PII for reporting needs
     - Shred PII data (any _non whitelisted_ data)
     - make patient read only?
  - PII Conversion
     -  Other Contact has data? -> set a flag
     - appt date changed? after pledge sent? -> set a flag
     - clinic changed?  after pledge sent? -> set a flag
     - other?
  - Outstanding Questions
     - 120 days past what? Initial Call? Appt Date? LMP?
     - how does the archive method get called? Button? Cron?
     - what does this do to views?
     - does this break patient field validations?
     - how to handle logs?
        - Kat leaning towards nuking them completely 

Comment 8 | created 2017-05-05T23:08:08Z
Source: https://github.com/DARIAEngineering/dcaf_case_management/issues/812#issuecomment-299595446
re: same patients linked somehow, I think the ideal here is that the same patients will share IDs, and we'll be able to group them by that. We can use `patient_identifier` for that, which we can generate by some scramble or some consistent business logic. This is a DCAF need (DCAF is interested in what repeat users of our service look like).

Patient read only would be great. I think if after archiving it requires rooting around in the rails console, that's a great outcome.

120 days should probably be after a pledge is sent. But we might want to crank that up. Let's set it at 120 past pledge until we come up a better plan though.

re: calling archive method, There's a nightly cleanup rake task that gets called which we can hook into; we can probably define this as a class method on Patient and call it from there. 

re: views, In a nutshell, they should stop being searchable.

re: validations, it'll blow up a lot of them, but rails will let us work around this use case by setting validations. See the current validation on the pregnancy model, for example, which fires certain validations IF an attribute is true -- we can do something similar for patient, enforcing phone/name if archived is false. 

+1 on nuking audit logs.

(See [De-anonymization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De-anonymization))

### Version

* vert.x core: 3.3.3
* vert.x auth: 3.3.3

### Context

MongoAuth provides a method to add a new User: 

    void insertUser(String username, String password, List<String> roles, List<String> permissions,
      Handler<AsyncResult<String>> resultHandler);

This approach does not provide any way to supply additional fields to the entry being saved. I suggest changing this method to add a JsonObject to which all data will be added before being stored:

    void insertUser(JsonObject template, String username, String password, List<String> roles, List<String> permissions,
      Handler<AsyncResult<String>> resultHandler);

the alternative is to work around in my code to insert a user via MongoAuth and then manually update the user with the needed data... (as any other user would have to do),,,

Comment 3 | created 2016-12-16T14:46:26Z
Source: https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vertx-auth/issues/102#issuecomment-267609141
I'd say that if you're passing a json object template the template itself should already contain the username and password:

```java
void insertUser(JsonObject template, List<String> roles, List<String> permissions,
  Handler<AsyncResult<String>> resultHandler);
```

WDYT?

Comment 4 | created 2016-12-16T14:46:51Z
Source: https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vertx-auth/issues/102#issuecomment-267609223
@stefanvitz feel free to discuss and make PRs

Comment 5 | created 2016-12-17T10:51:06Z
Source: https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vertx-auth/issues/102#issuecomment-267756241
@pmlopes I'd disagree for 2 reasons.

1) username and password are 2 things that MongoAuth tracks as special fields (MongoAuth knows which key they are stored under). So why merge username and password with the template, but leave out permissions and roles? Also, this would require the caller to also know the keys under which username and password are stored.

2) the password shouldn't be stored in the JSON. MongoAuth takes care of the hashing strategy and only stores the hash. Sure, it could replace the password out of the template and replace it with the hash, but that seems more error prone.

I'd suggest something like

```
void insertUser(JsonObject template, String username, String password, List<String> roles, List<String> permissions,  Handler<AsyncResult<String>> resultHandler) {
  //Throw error if username or password field are already specified in template
  //Throw error if roles/permissions are not null and are already specified in template
  //Functionality as it exists now.
}
```

I'm willing to make a PR if you agree with this approach and if you let me know what to do with the existing method? (Adjust it, remove it, leave it be)

Now I think we should only throw error if the generated fields exists and are different from the mongoauth managed ones. Say if the username is the same it could be ok not to throw error but ignore and continue, same for roles/permissions **BUT** not for passwords, that should always be managed by the auth provider.

WDYT?

Issue body:
While the README highlights the focus on privacy the resulting application sadly doesn't. I don't think it's intended so I hope that the report helps to start investigating the reasons for that and remove the tracks from the Code:

https://reports.exodus-privacy.eu.org/en/reports/69301/

The exodus report indicates that there are code signatures of 11 trackers/ad services involved. **Important: It doesn't mean they are active, but that's something that should be investigated**.

My idea where this comes from: Dependencies. Since I already mention I don't expect it to be intentional, there is likely that those trackers came as "side-loaded content" by one of the dependencies. Anyway, I think it's important to find and getting rid of them. Hope you get this fixed soon as the app is great! GPL :+1: 

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2019-04-06T16:57:07Z
Source: https://github.com/Flaque/quirk/issues/45#issuecomment-480519693
Ah, this is known about. You're correct, these come from dependencies. 

This app is build on Expo, which includes a whole bunch of libraries for building mobile apps. Included with [Expo is the SDK for Segment](https://docs.expo.io/versions/latest/sdk/segment/). Unfortunately there's no easy way to unbundle it. :/  

This app does not actually use those libraries and I have no plans to. But it does mean that when deploying to iOS, I'll have to state that [I use IDFA](https://docs.expo.io/versions/latest/distribution/app-stores/#ios-specific-guidelines), even though the app doesn't.

One of Segment's use case is to ship data from one place to another. So it's SDKs come with support for a whole bunch of destinations including marketing tools like the FB suite, Google analytics, etc. Which is why I'm guessing they show up in the exodus privacy report. 

For the moment, I think we're okay to keep it as it is. If Expo gives a non-Segment version, I'll switch to that. 


Comment 2 | created 2019-04-07T12:52:48Z
Source: https://github.com/Flaque/quirk/issues/45#issuecomment-480587645
So I did some further network analytics today and sadly, those trackers aren't just included by the framework, they are also active:

On every app start there are requests to:

- settings.crashlytics.com
- graph.facebook.com
- exp.host (maybe not a tracker)
- expo.io (maybe not a tracker)

No matter what, this includes data like the app name. Which means to facebook and Google is knows that a user installed this application. Given that the app has a medical background in one way or another, it's a bit disturbing to have this known to Facebook and Google.

I agree that his is a build system problem, but either way, you definitely need to mention it in the apps privacy policy (which might still conflicts with GDPR as there is no user consent for that) and in long term perspective should definitely get fixed by either switching the framework or finding another solution. Of course for now I can only say those things for the Android version, but I don't expect the iOS version to be fundamentally different.

Hope this helps to move things even more towards privacy :)

Comment 3 | created 2019-04-08T01:17:37Z
Source: https://github.com/Flaque/quirk/issues/45#issuecomment-480651839
Ah, so: `exp.host` and `expo.io` are the updating server from [expo.io](https://expo.io/), the framework and updating system Quirk uses. My understanding is Expo uses crashlytics to provide crash reports. Expo also comes prepackaged with access to facebooks apis for things like fb login. That said, the FB graph api isn't being used or setup; there's no API key or account setup afaik. 

So this is a problem with the build system; if you're concerned about this, you're welcome to fork the app or go submit an issue on https://github.com/expo/expo. 

> Which means to facebook and Google is knows that a user installed this application.

This info is already known, or at least it's known by Google. When you install an app via the Google Play Store, they know you installed it. This info is also known by Expo, since they're delivering the updates to the device. 

> you definitely need to mention it in the apps privacy policy

It is. [See here.](https://flaque.github.io/quirksite/privacy)

# just to clarify

Quirk is _not_ a privacy app. 

It's a Cognitive Behavioral Therapy app that does not store your personally identifiable information and does not use identifiable analytics. 

Privacy isn't a feature of Quirk, it's just the way I built it. I didn't store your mental health thoughts on a server because the risks of doing so are more dangerous than the value it would provide to the user. 

I don't use anonymous analytics to see what buttons your clicking on or how often you record something because I have no reason to. Quirk is a free, open source app with nothing to sell you. It has no ads or in-app purchases. It has nothing to optimize for. 

What I'm saying is that I have no moral objection to first party data collection. (Third-party data buying & selling is pretty scummy.) If for some reason Quirk needed me to anonymous tracking, I would have no concerns doing that. But it doesn't, so I thankfully don't have to.

Collected user data, especially PII, is like nuclear waste. It's a necessary byproduct of a lot of products, but should be carefully stored and you should work to accrue as little as possible.

Issue body:
I stumbled upon GoatCounter yesterday and am very impressed. (So long Matomo.) The only missing information I noticed is location by state/province. In Canada, USA, China etc, I think it's useful to be able to see what state people are visiting from.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2020-06-20T17:42:58Z
Source: https://github.com/arp242/goatcounter/issues/310#issuecomment-647025676
I am in the same situation. There is another issue (#56) that notes that location data is recorded, but not in the UI. Is there a way to at least get raw data in the meantime?

Comment 2 | created 2020-06-20T18:24:20Z
Source: https://github.com/arp242/goatcounter/issues/310#issuecomment-647029909
The GeoIP database comes in two forms: "cities" and "countries". It currently uses the Countries database which is about 1.8M (2.4M in the source code), which is a bit large bit still small enough to include in the source code. The Cities version is 29M, which would be >30M in the source code – which is too large IMO. Right now GoatCounter can run without any external dependencies, which is a nice feature I rather like, and I'd rather not lose that. One way to fix that is to create out own GeoDB file with just the data we need, which would vastly reduce the filesize for both cases.

Another issue is that we need to be kind-of careful not to record too much specific Personally Identifiable Information (PII). A Country name is probably okay since it's not *that* identifiable, but once you get down to city levels if becomes a lot more identifiable. Recording US states is probably okay, since it's a big country comparable to the EU, but for something like Ireland I'd rather not record the county – just "Ireland" is more than specific enough. So we'd need some special-fu logic there too instead of just "record it all".

And for a lot of people splitting out various US states provides little value, and may even be undesirable. Not sure how to best manage this UI-wise.

All-in-all, it's not a "oh, let me just do this in 2 hours"-kind of feature if we want to do it right. As always, I'm happy to accept patches but I think it's unlikely I'll work on this in the short term.

> Is there a way to at least get raw data in the meantime?

There is no "raw data" for this; it gets the location from the GeoIP DB based on the IP address, and the IP address is never stored. There is no way to get more specific information for past requests.

Comment 3 | created 2020-09-01T17:48:28Z
Source: https://github.com/arp242/goatcounter/issues/310#issuecomment-685028792
An important issue. Seeing "United States" is not very informative, as informative as seeing "Europe" or "EU." Being able to drill-down to City level would be great.

Comment 4 | created 2020-09-03T03:14:23Z
Source: https://github.com/arp242/goatcounter/issues/310#issuecomment-686224348
Like I mentioned @gabrielgggg, I think City level is too fine-grained both for reasons of privacy and UX, but yeah, US state would be good. I think the easiest way forward for this would be to create a new GeoIP database based on the "Cities" version but groups the cities by US state. I looked at this a while ago, but the tooling for all of this is a bit meh: they got some Perl library for this which can be used for this, but I'm not super familiar with Perl so all in all a bit time-consuming to get right.

Comment 5 | created 2020-12-28T10:01:20Z
Source: https://github.com/arp242/goatcounter/issues/310#issuecomment-751657728
Alright, this is now added: it records the region for every location, e.g. US state, which can be viewed by clicking on a country in the chart. Since this information wasn't collected before today and we have no way to get it, it will be "unknown" for entries before today.

Because some people may not want to collect this detailed information like I said before, you can enable/disable this in the "data collection" section on the settings that I added a few days ago; it's enabled by default.

This issue is still open as there's one part left to do: I want to be able to add a new (optional) dashboard chart which shows the regions for a particular country, so you can just add "View regions for US"; this requires a bit of work on the dashboard settings screen and I'll finish that up later this week.

As I mentioned, the expanded "City" version of the database is much larger than the Country (>60M), so you need to use `-geodb GeoLite2-City.mmdb` if you want to use this in a self-hosted installation. I looked a bit at creating a custom version which includes Country + Region information but not "City" and some other stuff we don't use, but I couldn't really get the Perl library to work, so 🤷‍♂️ Maybe I'll try again later.

@Archcry 
TLS 1.2 actually isn't safe... and that's the problem!

Please read e.g. Cisco's blog:

https://blogs.cisco.com/security/tls-1-3-and-forward-secrecy-count-us-in-and-heres-why

Security Fans are Forward Secrecy Fans

The goal of forward secrecy is to protect the secrecy of past sessions so that a session stays secret going forward. With TLS 1.2 and earlier versions, a bad actor who discovered a server’s private key could use it to decrypt network traffic that had been sent earlier. For example, suppose someone started recording encrypted traffic in our network on January 1st and then discovered a server’s private key on January 31st. That person could decrypt all of the server’s traffic and make off with the credit card numbers we entered yesterday, our lab results from last week, and our team’s patent application from the week before.

With the forward secrecy in TLS 1.3, there’s no longer a single secret value that will decrypt multiple sessions. Instead, TLS 1.3 uses the Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol, which generates a one-time key that’s used only for the current network session. At the end of the session, the key is discarded. While attackers can still record and store encrypted network traffic, to decode it they need the unique key for each session. A session key won’t decode data sent during an earlier session or help an attacker discover future session keys.

Forward secrecy is a best practice for security—which is why we’re all for it.

+FROM alpine:edge
 
 LABEL maintainer="NGINX Docker Maintainers <docker-maint@nginx.com>"
 
@@ -52,11 +52,12 @@ RUN GPG_KEYS=B0F4253373F8F6F510D42178520A9993A1C052F8 \
        " \
        && addgroup -S nginx \
        && adduser -D -S -h /var/cache/nginx -s /sbin/nologin -G nginx nginx \
+       && echo "http://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/edge/testing" >> /etc/apk/repositories \
        && apk add --no-cache --virtual .build-deps \

@@ -33,13 +33,13 @@ RUN set -x \
        && case "$dpkgArch" in \
                amd64|i386) \
 # arches officialy built by upstream
-                       echo "deb https://nginx.org/packages/mainline/debian/ stretch nginx" >> /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nginx.list \
+                       echo "deb https://nginx.org/packages/mainline/ubuntu/ cosmic nginx" >> /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nginx.list \
                        && apt-get update \
                        ;; \
                *) \
 # we're on an architecture upstream doesn't officially build for
 # let's build binaries from the published source packages
-                       echo "deb-src https://nginx.org/packages/mainline/debian/ stretch nginx" >> /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nginx.list \

                        \
 # new directory for storing sources and .deb files
                        && tempDir="$(mktemp -d)" \

```

If anyone is interested (I know this is not a support forum, but maybe it is helpfull):
My problem was, that I did not specified a default_server so the behaviour of nginx is to use the first defined server. This is important cause ssllabs does not use SNI for its tests and so your "default server" answers. And if you don't have you ssl settings right there, it seems that TLS1.3 is not enabled.
Sorry for the noise.

Issue title: Implement Perfect Forward Secrecy for search queries
Project: searx/searx
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['privacy notice']"
GitHub labels: ["question", "security"]
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 3; discussants: 3
Reported: 2018-09-07 21:04:20+00; last active: 2020-10-26 11:25:39+00
Issue number: 1391

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 3/3
Scope: Current retrievable issue body and issue comments; not the original study's historical snapshot. Linked pages and attachments are not fetched.

Issue body:
Another metasearch engine called [Search Encrypt](https://www.searchencrypt.com) claims to use Perfect Forward Secrecy to protect search query privacy:

>  What encryption methods does Search Encrypt use?
> All requests to Search Encrypt are done over SSL. We utilize the latest encryption technologies, including a feature known as Perfect Forward Secrecy which goes a step further than traditional SSL by using a unique public key for each individual session. This means that each user receives a unique public key which improves security considerably. We also encrypt the local queries using a client side encryption utilizing a short lived key which helps to protect browser history.

> After you’ve finished your searching, the encryption key for your search term expires so it is essentially gone forever.

If I understand this correctly then if someone were to unknowingly use a malicious Searx instance that logs requests to later sell to a 3rd party, if this were implemented they would no longer be able to decrypt these requests at a later date.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2018-09-16T11:32:13Z
Source: https://github.com/searx/searx/issues/1391#issuecomment-421749664
What Search Encrypt is describing is the connection between the browser and Search Encrypt servers.

[EDIT] Forward Secrecy add an additional layer of protection on HTTPS : if someone records the encrypted packets between your browser and Search Encrypt, cracking one connection doesn't help to crack the other connections. Forward secrecy doesn't prevent Search Encrypt to log all requests.

To compare, let's see the usual Searx setup :

```
Browser ---[ HTTPS ] --->{ Reverse Proxy ---> Searx }---[ HTTPS ] ---> duckduckgo / google / etc...
```
Reverse Proxy can be Apache, Nginx, haproxy, nghttp2, etc...

The forward secrecy configuration is up to administrator of the Searx instance (the reverse proxy configuration).

You can see the Qualys SSL Lab score for each Searx instance here : https://stats.searx.xyz/

Example with searx.xyz :
https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/analyze.html?d=searx.xyz
There is Forward Secrecy for all ciphers (In Cipher Suites section, there is "FS" for each cipher).
Of course doing so means searx.xyz is not available to old browsers.

About www.searchencrypt.com : 
https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/analyze.html?d=www.searchencrypt.com

Some cipher doesn't support Forward Secrecy.
Basically if you use a mordern Firefox / Chrome / Safari you will use Forward Secrecy, but you are not sure with old browser.

So either : 
* you are sure to use Forward Secrecy, if it is not possible you won't be able to access the web site (searx.xyz, searx.me, and some other Searx instances)
* you are most probably using Forward Secrecy if you are using a modern browser ( www.searchencrypt.com, google.com)

Another point is the encrypted search queries of SearchEncrypt : 
the search queries are encrypted using AES and a random key (see https://www.searchencrypt.com/js/search ) 
The AES parameters are stored in two differents cookies (EncKey and EncToken).
So the request is in clear on the wire as any other search engine ( eyedropper can't them since there is HTTPS ).

So why encrypting the search queries ?
* no browser history if the cookies are changed : require some tests, I don't know when the keys change, the cookies doesn't seems to expire.
* Search Encrypt server logs won't contains the query : most on the time logs contains the URL not the cookies. Not really helpful since Search Encrypt has the query anyway.

Searx solves this in different way : it uses the POST HTTP method. 
The URL remains the same, but the query is sent using the HTTP body of the request.

There is glitch about Searx : despite using the POST HTTP method, the HTML title contains the search query, that's mean the browser will contains the different search queries.
See https://github.com/asciimoo/searx/issues/1011 (issue solved with the simple theme).

Some other technical notes about SearchEncrypt :
* web server host by Amazon, running using Microsoft-IIS.
* HTTPS certificate issued by Amazon.
* The EncKey / EncToken cookies can be used as a user identifier (once again it depends when there are changed).

Moreover see the privacy notice of SearchEncrypt, section "What information we collect and how we collect it." : 
https://www.searchencrypt.com/legal/privacy

About Searx, if you are worried about Forward Secrecy from Searx to the different engines, see https://github.com/asciimoo/searx/pull/931 for some technical details.

To sum up it's about who you trust, what is the threat model / what are you afraid of ?

Side note : I don't know how SearchEncrypt provides results ? does it use another search engine ?

Comment 2 | created 2018-09-16T19:44:32Z
Source: https://github.com/searx/searx/issues/1391#issuecomment-421820598
@dalf ah I see, thanks for your very comprehensive explanation! My takeaway is that SearchEncrypt is just using marketing jargon when in reality not all of their ciphers do have FS whereas Searx in contrast has FS for all of theirs.  

SE is a metasearch engine so it uses Google etc like Searx. 

The threat model I have is to limit the amount of information both the metasearch engine and the search engines themselves have about me. By using a metasearch engine anonymity can be gained compared to using the search engine directly, but then the metasearch engine has full info about the query.

I was mainly hoping for a some sort of E2E encryption for queries, so that the metasearch engine relays the queries and gets results but is at no point aware of what the query was. 

Comment 3 | created 2020-10-26T11:25:38Z
Source: https://github.com/searx/searx/issues/1391#issuecomment-716486403
> I was mainly hoping for a some sort of E2E encryption for queries, so that the metasearch engine relays the queries and gets results but is at no point aware of what the query was.

The point of searx is that it knows the search query and handles the interaction with search engines. 
Query encryption and forward secrecy isn't really an issue in case of searx, because it is a free software and anybody can use or host a trusted instance.

 ​Cloudflare uses various cookies to maximize network resources, manage traffic, and protect our customers’ sites from malicious traffic. 
  
 ​##​ ​Understanding the Cloudflare Cookies 
  
 ​As defined in our [​Privacy Policy​](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/), the ​`__cflb`​, ​`__cf_bm`​, ​`cf_ob_info`​ and ​`cf_use_ob`​, ​`__cfwaitingroom`​, and ​`__cfruid`​ cookies are strictly necessary to provide the services requested by our customers. 
  
 ​As mentioned in our Privacy Policy, Cloudflare encourages our customers to disclose the use of these cookies to their end users and, in some jurisdictions, customers may be required by law to disclose these cookies to their end users. 
  
 ​Cookie data is processed in Cloudflare's data center in the United States and is subject to the cross-border data transfer section 7 of the Cloudflare [​Privacy Policy​](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/). 
  
 ​###​ ​\_\_​cflb cookie for Cloudflare Load Balancer session affinity 
  
 ​When enabling session affinity with [​Cloudflare Load Balancer​](/load-balancing/understand-basics/session-affinity/), Cloudflare sets a ​`__cflb`​ cookie with a unique value on the first response to the requesting client. Cloudflare routes future requests to the same origin, optimizing network resource usage. In the event of a failover, Cloudflare sets a new ​`__cflb`​ cookie to direct future requests to the failover pool. 
  
 ​The ​`__cflb`​ cookie allows Cloudflare to return an end user to the same customer origin for a specific period of time configured by the customer. This allows the end user to have a seamless experience (for example, this cookie is used for keeping an end user’s items in a shopping cart while they continue to navigate around the website). This cookie is a session cookie that lasts from several seconds up to 24 hours. 
  
 ​{{<Aside type="note">}} 
  
 ​Currently Cloudflare only supports Session Affinity in "orange-cloud" (proxied) mode. 
  
 ​{{</Aside>}} 
  
 ​###​ ​\_\_​cf_bm cookie for Cloudflare bot products 
  
 ​Cloudflare's [​bot products​](/bots/) identify and mitigate automated traffic to protect your site from bad bots. Cloudflare places the ​`__cf_bm`​ cookie on end-user devices that access customer sites protected by Bot Management or Bot Fight Mode. The ​`__cf_bm`​ cookie is necessary for these bot solutions to function properly. 
  
 ​This cookie expires after 30 minutes of continuous inactivity by the end user. The cookie contains information related to the calculation of Cloudflare’s proprietary bot score and, when Anomaly Detection is enabled on Bot Management, a session identifier. The information in the cookie (other than time-related information) is encrypted and can only be decrypted by Cloudflare. 
  
 ​A separate ​`__cf_bm`​ cookie is generated for each site that an end user visits, as Cloudflare does not track users from site to site or from session to session. The ​`__cf_bm`​ cookie is generated independently by Cloudflare, and does not correspond to any user ID or other identifiers in a customer’s web application. 
  
 ​{{<Aside type="note">}} 
  
 ​Bot Management is available to Enterprise customers as an add-on service. Contact your Cloudflare account team to enable Bot Management for your site. Non-Enterprise customers can enable [​Bot Fight Mode or Super Bot Fight Mode​](/bots/). 
  
 ​{{</Aside>}} 
  
 ​###​ ​cf_ob_info and cf_use_ob cookie for Cloudflare Always Online 
  
 ​The ​`cf_ob_info`​ cookie provides information on: 
  
 ​-​ The HTTP Status Code returned by the origin web server 
 ​-​ The Ray ID of the original failed request 
 ​-​ The data center serving the traffic 
  
 ​The ​`cf_use_ob`​ cookie informs Cloudflare to fetch the requested resource from the Always Online cache on the designated port. Applicable values are: 0, 80, and 443. The ​`cf_ob_info`​ and ​`cf_use_ob`​ cookies are persistent cookies that expire after 30 seconds. 
  
 ​###​ ​\_\_​cfwaitingroom for Cloudflare Waiting Rooms 
  
 ​[​Cloudflare’s Waiting Room​](/waiting-room/) product enables a waiting room for a particular host and path combination within a zone. Visitors are put in the waiting room and provided an estimate of when they will be allowed to access the application, if not immediately available. 
  
 ​The ​`__cfwaitingroom`​ cookie is only used to track visitors that access a Waiting Room enabled host and path combination for a zone. Visitors using a browser that does not accept cookies cannot visit the host and path combination while the Waiting Room is active. For more details, see [​Waiting Room cookie​](/waiting-room/reference/waiting-room-cookie/). 
  
 ​###​ ​\_\_​cfruid to support Cloudflare Rate Limiting Products 
  
 ​The ​`__cfruid`​ cookie is strictly necessary to support Cloudflare Rate Limiting products. As part of our Rate Limiting solution, this cookie is required to manage incoming traffic and to have better visibility on the origin of a particular request. 
  
 ​###​ ​Additional cookies used by the Challenge Platform 
  
 ​The table below shows additional cookies used by the Challenge Platform. 
  
 ​| Cookie Name (XXX represents dynamic part)                     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                   | 
 ​| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 
 ​| `cf_clearance`                                                | Clearance Cookie stores the proof of challenge passed. It is used to no longer issue a captcha or jschallenge challenge if present. It is required to reach origin server.                    | 
 ​| `cf-cc-XXX`; `cf-chl-cc-XXX`; `cf-chl-seq-XXX`; `cf-chl-prog` | These cookies are used by Cloudflare for the execution of Javascript or Captcha challenges. They are not used for tracking or beyond the scope of the challenge. They can be deleted if seen. | 
 ​| `cf-chl-XXXX`                                                 | This cookie is used to check whether the [Cloudflare Edge server](https://www.cloudflare.com/en-gb/learning/cdn/glossary/edge-server/) supports cookies. It can be deleted if seen.           | 
 ​| `cf-chl-rc-i`; `cf-chl-rc-ni`                                 | These cookies are for internal use which allows Cloudflare to identify production issues on clients.                                                                                          | 
  
 ​##​ ​Related resources 
  
 ​-​ [​Understanding SameSite cookie interaction with Cloudflare​](https://support.cloudflare.com/hc/articles/360038470312)

Issue body:
The netdata installer says the following:

```
  The following changes will be made to your system:

  # USERS / GROUPS
  User 'netdata' and group 'netdata' will be added, if not present.

  # LOGROTATE
  This file will be installed if logrotate is present.

   - /etc/logrotate.d/netdata

  # SYSTEM INIT
  This file will be installed if this system runs with systemd:

   - /lib/systemd/system/netdata.service

   or, for older Centos, Debian/Ubuntu or OpenRC Gentoo:

   - /etc/init.d/netdata         will be created


  This package can also update a netdata installation that has been
  created with another version of it.

  Your netdata configuration will be retained.
  After installation, netdata will be (re-)started.

  netdata re-distributes a lot of open source software components.
  Check its full license at:
  https://github.com/netdata/netdata/blob/master/LICENSE.md
Please type y to accept, n otherwise:
```

However, it does not tell me that it's going to silently spy on me.  I don't consent to analytics.  It spied on me and sent my data away without my consent.  I had to uninstall it, clean my system, and reinstall it using an obscure, barely-documented flag.

This is not respecting user consent.  Notify the user before spying on them, if you intend to do so, so they have an opportunity to cancel and delete your software if they don't wish for that to happen.

Comment 1 | created 2019-11-25T15:50:42Z

Comment 2 | created 2019-11-25T16:05:28Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558222961
Hi @sneak,

The info regarding telemetry has been prominently featured in the [Anonymous Statistics](https://docs.netdata.cloud/docs/anonymous-statistics/) section of our documentation, it is part of our [Privacy policy](https://docs.netdata.cloud/docs/privacy-policy/), it's mentioned in the [Security documentation](https://docs.netdata.cloud/docs/netdata-security/#opt-out-of-anonymous-statistics) and displayed in a [`netdata-installer.sh` message](https://github.com/netdata/netdata/blob/master/netdata-installer.sh#L866)

These places have the information, because users requested it to be there, in order to make it prominent. We have never denied a request to improve visibility into telemetry and you're welcome to do a PR to improve the text of the particular installer (files are under `packaging/makeself`).

We don't appreciate the term "spying", as we have done our best to prevent to ensure that no  information that could identify any users or specific systems is transmitted and continue to accept recommendations on how to make this clearer. We do not intend however to change telemetry to opt-in, as we need at least some basic aggregated metrics, to help us make decisions (e.g. on the OS versions that we need to prioritize in our binary packaging distros and test automation).

Comment 3 | created 2019-11-25T16:09:07Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558224606
> we have done our best to prevent to ensure that no information that could identify any users or specific systems is transmitted and continue to accept recommendations on how to make this clearer. 

This is an objectively false statement.  The user's IP address, which is personally identifying information (PII) is transmitted with the analytics.  Google receives the user's usage data, *plus* their IP address, which is identifying.

The fact that the data that you collect by spying is useful to you does not make it not spying.  The fact that Google doesn't provide *you* with the IP address information doesn't mean that personally identifying information isn't being transmitted.  Those are facts, not opinion.

> We do not intend however to change telemetry to opt-in, as we need at least some basic aggregated metrics, to help us make decisions 

You don't *need* that information, you *want* that information.  It's reasonable to want that information.  What's not reasonable is to pretend that you're not violating user consent.

Fact: **I was given no opportunity to opt out, no notice that my identifying information would be transmitted before your software did so.**  I followed the instructions on your website and your software spied on me, without my knowledge or consent.

Don't take my word for it: try it!  Spin up a brand new VM and run the command on the frontpage of your website to install:

`bash <(curl -Ss https://my-netdata.io/kickstart.sh)`

Guess what?  No notification.  No option to opt out.  Nothing - just the transmission of my personally identifiable information to Google.

Comment 4 | created 2019-11-25T18:22:23Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558279022
@sneak you are right that we need to make it clear that anonymous statistics are by default enabled. @cakrit please make sure we add the relative information everywhere. Also, the kickstart script requires an ENTER to be pressed, so please make sure anonymous statistics logs a line at that point, before actually installing anything.

@sneak however, you have a misunderstanding on PII. It is actually a common misunderstanding among most engineers (even security engineers), and I think it comes from the fact that GDPR considers IPs as PII.

IP addresses, phone numbers, etc are PII only when they can be potentially correlated with your identity, that is only when someone can somehow relate this IP, phone number, etc to your name. If this correlation cannot happen, the IPs are just IPs, not PII.

In our case, this correlation cannot be done. We do not have any means to correlate the IP address with any person.

Of course, you may think that we can't, but probably Google can. For this case, complying with GDPR, GA has an option to anonymize IPs. We have enabled this option, so even Google cannot correlate IPs with your identity.

Our intention is never to spy our users and we will comply with anything required in that respect.

Yes, for users in places where GDPR applies. Let’s also not forget about the practices of the intelligence services (thank you, Ed Snowden!) in the country in which Google operates. They don’t give two fucks about four fucks about what the GDPR says is or isn’t legal. 

**It is not, and will never be anonymous.**

...but that’s fine, because if you get consent first, you’ll be all good. 

Comment 9 | created 2019-11-25T18:50:06Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558289867
We can squabble all day about what is or isn’t PII: you didn’t have my consent when your software made my computer connect to Google. It wasn’t what I wanted when I installed a locally-hosted monitoring package. It wasn’t disclosed. 

You can get just barely on the right side of ethical by disclosing it clearly first and forcing a user to control-c, but why not just *ask* for consent? 

Are you afraid that too many people would say no? If that’s the case, using your analytics data *today* is unethical, based on the assumption that most users would say “please do not spy on me” when asked directly. 

Just ask during install. It’ll be fine. 

Comment 10 | created 2019-11-25T19:00:28Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558294006
> Are you afraid that too many people would say no? If that’s the case, using your analytics data _today_ is unethical, based on the assumption that most users would say “please do not spy on me” when asked directly.

No, this is not the case. We don't want any questions or any configuration during install. This is the whole point with netdata. One command, no questions, done!

We are always trying to give sane defaults. There are hundreds of thousands of options available, but for everything we ship sane defaults.

So, we want anonymous statistics enabled by default, we don't want to ask questions, but we should let people know this is the default and how to change it, even before installation.

Comment 11 | created 2019-11-25T19:29:14Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558304905
> We don't want any questions or any configuration during install. 

You are already asking a question (asking for consent even) **today** during install, as shown above, which makes me question whether or not this is even a good faith discussion. 

> We are always trying to give sane defaults.

A sane default would be not to use a computer’s resources to send surveillance to Google unless you are absolutely, positively sure—beforehand—that the owner of that computer is okay with that. 

Seeing as you’re already fine with asking questions (QED) before modifying a user’s system during install, I don’t see how asking for permission is onerous or difficult.

Comment 12 | created 2019-11-25T20:10:39Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558321068
The only question there is today is like this:

```
We will do the following:

- this
- that
- the other

If you agree, press ENTER > 
```

So, in the list we will also include the anonymous statistics status.
I think this will be enough.

If we start adding individual questions, then a lot of people will start requesting all kinds of things to be decided before installation, like "do you want to enable a registry? do you want to enable netdata.cloud? do you want collect security metrics? do you want to enable statsd? do you want the api to be enabled by default?" and many, many, many more.

The only sane answer to all those questions, is that we ship sane defaults, and we never ask questions. A good overview is all that is required and proper instructions so that everyone will know what will get.

Comment 13 | created 2019-11-25T21:46:38Z
Source: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7366#issuecomment-558354433
You’re in charge; you get to say “yes, we should ask for consent for uploading telemetry because privacy belongs to the user, however we will say no to asking other configuration questions because we want to keep the experience streamlined.” The fact that you ask for consent for telemetry is fine, *because it is unethical not to*, and you can continue to deny users who ask for other, non-consent-critical additional configuration options at install time without being inconsistent in your reasoning. 

Respecting user consent and privacy rights does not mean that you have to agree to do every poorly-informed feature that someone else demands of you, simply because the UI is similar for both. 

If you make the opt-out option clear in the message right there under the notification, all you’re going to do is make most users (who don’t want to be spied on) press a more keys: ^C, up arrow, space, disable telemetry flag, enter. (If they see it, that is - I suggest making it bold because there’s already a lot of text on that confirmation screen.)

It’s not simpler; it’s actually a lot more complex. And in the minority case (those who don’t mind the privacy loss), you’re only saving them one keystroke.

> *So, in the list we will also include the anonymous statistics status.*

Please stop calling them that. **It is not, and will never be anonymous.** Calling it anonymous is a **false statement**. Google receives the data, as well as *personally identifying information* in the form of an IP address and timestamp. Any other organizations that have access to Google’s data (legally or otherwise: ISPs, carriers, hosting providers, intelligence services, rogue employees, et c) receive the *personally identifying information*, as well. 

The fact that *you* do not receive the IP and timestamp data is not relevant to the privacy invasion and danger of its collection. The fact that *you* cannot correlate it to a person is also not relevant.

Just my two cents, I'm no lawyer, I use GA minimally on my own websites, but the whole point of GDPR is that people are considered opted OUT by default, they must choose to opt in and there has to be a record of them doing so. The clock reset on GDPR launch day. 

There also can be nothing vague or unclear in the provision of the question (a tiny checkbox, small print, hard to disguise colours etc). From newsletters, to analytics, it doesn't matter what the format is. If you provide services to anyone in the EU, whether free or otherwise, you have to respect that underlying principle of GDPR. Yes, GDPR is a PITA but it's a necessary evil and inconvenience these days. It's afterall about giving people back control over their data and information and to be honest, if you have tens of thousands of users that you are collecting data from, you definitely need to make sure everything is 100% correct!

There is nothing wrong with reviewing the decision or ensuring your understanding, in fact it's a requirement to regularly review your GDPR policy, say once a year to ensure it's relevant, up to date, you still have a recognised reason for collecting the data etc. It's great to see this has been flagged as needing triage, that being open and transparent.

So if I might make a suggestion, immediately disable GA. Review your GDPR compliance. Then if you don't want to have the installer stopping to ask if users if they want to opt in to Google Analytics, then either have two clearly marked installers (one without GA enabled and one with), or disable GA by default and let users OPT IN via changing a setting in netdata.conf.

The command virtualenv is provided by a Python package that enable the creation of these virtual environments. You can install virtualenv using you packaging system. Imagine we have a community using a chat system not only to share cat picz but to build something great towards a big goal. Like an open source or an open hardware project. In the process we share valuable **knowledge** and ideas in this chat. In other words, we rely on chat for something serious. Now consider the same scenario for two systems. A: Any decade-old IRC or XMPP client: 1. enable saving of chat logs to local text files 2. chat with your community for years, accumulating knowledge 3. the single server we all used is gone (for whatever reason) Result: a lot of members have replicas of community's entire chat history and can cooperate to quickly respawn it in a new location. B: Matrix flagship client (Element) in 2020: 1. chat with your community for years, accumulating knowledge 2. the single server we all used is gone (for whatever reason) Result: there is a high chance that everything is lost. Do homeservers replicate the entirety of _all_ rooms or only slices of rooms relevant to homeserver's users? I didn't study other Matrix clients but I assume it is the same for many. Now I open matrix.org: > An open network for secure, **decentralized** communication and > Matrix is really a decentralised conversation store rather than a messaging protocol. and so on. Considering the practical difficulty of running homeservers let me ask a simple question: What is more decentralized? a. 1 central IRC server + 10 always-online users that save chat logs and publish them somewhere + 50 users who periodically sync them b. 1-3 Matrix homeservers you will find in small communities + **0** users saving chat logs I should also mention that in the IRC scenario it is practically impossible to delete messages from users' local files. In Matrix it is possible to delete messages and while I hope the database is append-only, I'm not sure it is possible for users to recover deleted messages in all cases. Closing my mini-rant, Matrix is the best open-source, actively-developed, semi-decentralized, self-hosted, E2EE-enabled chat system I am aware of. I highly respect what Matrix is doing and I am very thankful that we now have a decent alternative to Slack/Discord/Telegram where freedom and sovereignty mean something. The point of this message is to make a case that from a _user perspective_, as it is today, Matrix is **less decentralized** than IRC. I don't want to sound too negative, but such system is _training_ end users to rely on servers and believe/hope everything will be fine. Issue body:
A typical problem in multi-journal installations is that a user has registered to journal A and later want's to submit something to journal B as well. However, usually this is not possible, because the user does not have the author role in journal B.

I made a feature request about how OJS should handle this situation. http://forum.pkp.sfu.ca/t/ojs3-missing-author-roles-in-multi-journal-installations/28710

In my opinion having a simple button to enable the author role in that message would be ideal. However, I developed a quick fix where the message text has an additional link leading to the user profile/roles page. This will probably help in most cases. PR in a minute.
