Issue body:
### 1. Cookie Without SameSite Flag Detected
When the SameSite flag is set on a cookie, the browser will prevent it from being sent along with cross-site requests. This can help prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. |
Remediation path: If the cookie contains sensitive information, then the server should ensure that the cookie has the SameSite flag set. This flag can have two values: strict or lax. With the strict value the cookie will only be sent if the request originates from the same website. With the lax value the cookie will only be sent for GET requests.
References: https://www.owasp.org/index.php/SameSite
### ~2. Cookie Without Secure Flag Detected~
~When the `secure` flag is set on a cookie, the browser will prevent it from being sent over a clear text channel (HTTP) and only allow it to be sent when an encrypted channel is used (HTTPS). The scanner discovered that a cookie was set by the server without the secure flag being set. Although the initial setting of this cookie was via an HTTPS connection, any HTTP link to the same server will result in the cookie being sent in clear text. Note that if the cookie does not contain sensitive information, the risk of this vulnerability is mitigated.~
~Remediation path: If the cookie contains sensitive information, then the server should ensure that the cookie has the `secure` flag set.~
~References:~
~https://www.owasp.org/index.php/SecureFlag~

Moved #2 to #3102

Released issue metadata:
Issue title: Proposal to change the default handling of Purpose 4 in the TCF v2.0 enforcement updates
Project: prebid/Prebid.js
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['CCPA']"
GitHub labels: []
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 9; discussants: 4
Reported: 2020-05-05 14:29:09+00; last active: 2020-06-01 17:36:24+00
Issue number: 5194

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 9/9
Scope: Retrieval-time original issue/comment Markdown from GitHub's structured page data; full discussion only when count and pagination checks pass. Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately.

Issue body:
# Background
A proposal has been made to the Prebid project to enforce some elements of the IAB’s TCF v2.0 within Prebid.js and Prebid Server (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fBRaodKifv1pYsWY3ia-9K96VHUjd8kKvxZlOsozm8E/edit#heading=h.hlpacpauqwkx). The goal is to add “basic enforcement” of the GDPR in order to confirm that there's enough evidence of consent to pass data on to vendors who have access to the GVL and can fully parse and enforce.  As part of this proposal, Purpose 4 of the IAB TCF v2.0 was included as an enforceable purpose. Purpose 4 is known as "Personalized Ad Selection" and defined as “Select personalised ads based on a user profile or other historical user data, including a user’s prior activity, interests, visits to sites or apps, location, or demographic information”. Basically, if the user doesn’t consent, they don’t want ads based on any type of user profile.

# The Original Proposal for Purpose 4
The proposal says that if the user does not consent to Purpose 4 for a particular vendor, then no user ids (`user.buyeruid`, `user.id`, `user.ext.eids`, `user.ext.digitrust`, `device.ifa`, `device.macsha1`, `device.macmd5`, `device.dpidsha1`, `device.dpidmd5`, `device.didsha1`, `device.didmd5`) will be sent to the demand partner via their bid adapter (PBJS) or bid request (PBS). 

### Concerns with the Default Setting in the Proposal
The concern with this approach is that there are valid reasons for a buyer to receive a user ID even if they will not have the consent to use the ID for Personalized Ad Selection.

#### Purpose 2: Basic Ad Selection
Assuming Purpose 2 is consented to...Without a user identifier, the buyer won’t be able to frequency or recency cap their campaigns, actions that are allowed per the TCF v2.0 guidance: “To select basic ads vendors can: ... Control the frequency of ads shown to a user; Sequence the order in which ads are shown to a user…” (https://iabeurope.eu/iab-europe-transparency-consent-framework-policies/#Purpose_2__Select_basic_ads_).

#### Purpose 7: Measure Ad Performance
Assuming Purpose 7 is consented to...Without a user identifier, the buyer won’t be able to measure the performance and effectiveness of ads that it purchased. This includes activities such as measuring unique users reached or ad attribution, conversions, and sales lift. These actions are allowed per the TCF v2.0 guidance (https://iabeurope.eu/iab-europe-transparency-consent-framework-policies/#Purpose_7__Measure_ad_performance).

### Workaround
The implementation of TCF v2.0 within Prebid.js is such that exceptions can be made by the publisher to bypass the default settings. In this case, if a publisher would like to pass all userIds, or just userIds for specific vendors from the userId module, regardless of Purpose 4 consent signals, they can do so with some config.

While the workaround does exist, the default setting will be used by most publishers and will lead to under-monetized inventory. If a publisher chooses to, they can use the same system of exceptions to remove userIds when the user has not granted consent for Purpose 4.

# Counter Proposal for Purpose 4
I propose that the default behavior when Purpose 4 does not have consent by the user is to still share userIds with demand partners. If publishers don't want to use this behavior, they can use the exceptions configuration to block userIds for all or specific vendors that they choose.

# Other Privacy Flags
It’s worth noting that in Prebid Server, `user.ext.eids` are removed for COPPA, CCPA, LMT, and DNT, currently with no vendor exceptions mechanism like is available for the GDPR. While there may be valid use cases to send userIds in some of these cases, without an exceptions mechanism, the right thing to do is block all userIds as are being done today.

I find Scott's case persuasive in the case of purpose 2 or 7 consent. Id's seem integral to those purposes. 

In the case of the auction beginning before the user interacts with the cmp (when the timeout is hit),
it seems like it might be reasonable for id modules to self-select as publisher generated ids or third party ids, in which case id5 and pubcid and potentially other submodules ( I am aware of at least one other similar proposed identifier that doesn't yet have a submodule PR) would be publisher generated ids. 

However, Prebid core would then have to become aware of what is publisher generated and what is not, and that may be subject to debate for certain submodules, so passing id's when none of 2,4,and 7 consent exists seems like it would be difficult to maintain as a default state. It it were the default state, it seems it would then be incumbant on Prebid reviewers to be responsible for policing id modules as pub generated or not and edge cases such as pub.direct would be difficult to decide. 

In summary, it seems reasonable to pass id's when any of 2,4,7 exists, but at least one of them, as passing them when none exists would require impossible classification of id's into two groups that is better left to the publisher than prebid reviewers.

Comment 6 | created 2020-05-07T07:55:21Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/5194#issuecomment-625093831
Hi @jaiminpanchal27 - My understanding of the original proposal from @bretg is that if no rules are defined by the publisher AND the user does not consent to purpose 4 (but does consent to purpose 1 and 2), then user ids would NOT be sent to bid adapters. My proposal here is that in this case, user ids would be sent to bid adapters.

In your example, the publisher has explicitly defined a rule to enforce purpose 4 across all vendors, which is slightly different I think. 

I would still make the argument that userIds are completely valid in this scenario, per my arguments earlier. In fact, I'm not entirely sure I agree with PBJS doing any enforcement around Purpose 4 because the logic for whether ads are selected for personalization or not is completely dependent on the bidding platform's internal logic, nothing that can be determined ahead of time (and, given that I'd argue user ids are valid when not using personalization, they are still valid for all demand partners). 

That said...I'm open to considering enforcement such that if a publisher puts in a rule as you described for Purpose 4, then usersyncs would be blocked and userIds would be stripped. If a publisher wanted to allow certain vendor usersyncs or userIds, they could add the necessary exceptions to the rule.

Comment 7 | created 2020-05-18T14:59:52Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/5194#issuecomment-630240580
We met last week and have significantly revised the proposed handling of TCF2 defaults. See https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fBRaodKifv1pYsWY3ia-9K96VHUjd8kKvxZlOsozm8E/edit# -- will leave the changes highlighted for a week or so

Comment 8 | created 2020-05-20T01:20:32Z
Source: https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/issues/5194#issuecomment-631176963
The committee met again and approved the following:

1) Purpose 4 does not imply the removal of User Ids
2) Prebid.js will not remove User IDs. This is left up to server-side code which can deal with the IAB Global Vendor List
3) Prebid Server will remove User IDs when there is no legal basis for any Purpose from 2-10. Purpose 1 is device access, which is about setting User IDs, not using them. Prebid Server will not consider whether the host company or account are enforcing a given purpose when determining legal basis for P2-10.
4) Prebid.js will block head bidding auctions if there's no legal basis test for Purpose 2, *including legitmate interest established*
5) Prebid.js will default to enforcing Purposes 1 and 2 if those rules aren't defined.
6) Other than these changes, everything else stays the same. However, it means the PBJS [Purpose 2 Pull Request](https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/pull/5185) needs to change the [Purpose 4 PR](https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/pull/5228) gets closed. And there are changes for Prebid Server.

Comment 1 | created 2016-10-26T23:41:22Z
Source: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/109#issuecomment-256508258
What would be the implications of deleting an account from the technical perspective?

It would be problematic, for example, if someone could immediately register a new account with the same username. Remote instances that may not be aware of the account's prior deletion would keep following the new, now impersonating account.

So the username needs to stick around after deletion. Then every status by the user would be deleted, every deletion would need to be federated which might take a while (imagine deleting 40,000 statuses - you'd need to send the updated "deleted" status for every remote follower x 40,000).

So this solution would be a soft delete then - as much information as possible is removed but basic structure and some pointers must be retained. So perhaps we could delete avatar, display name, bio, delete all statuses/media, unfollow everyone the account has been following, force all local users to unfollow it (cannot force remote accounts to unfollow though). Perhaps disable login on the account.

That's quite a big task, isn't it

@planet4589 : the email comparison isn't good, because emails are private. A better and accurate comparison is with content you published on a website. 

You definitively can ask the owner of a website to delete the content you published on her website, because you own the copyright of your toots. 

Unless you agreed to specific terms of service or published your toots under a free license, the owner has to delete your content, or you can sue them. It may be unpractical and excessive to go that far, yet it's important for instance providers to note that the law is by default on the side of the person who wants to leave the service.

Users should be provided with an option to require automatically all the federated instances to delete their content, because doing it manually is virtually impossible. It means that there is a high cost of leaving, which is a disservice to the growth of the project.

@ajanvier same requirements are listed on current EU law. http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1493967534436&uri=CELEX:32016R0679

<details>
	<summary>Law text</summary>

> A data subject should have the right to have personal data concerning him or her rectified and a ‘right to be forgotten’ where the retention of such data infringes this Regulation or Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject. In particular, a data subject should have the right to have his or her personal data erased and no longer processed where the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are collected or otherwise processed, where a data subject has withdrawn his or her consent or objects to the processing of personal data concerning him or her, or where the processing of his or her personal data does not otherwise comply with this Regulation. That right is relevant in particular where the data subject has given his or her consent as a child and is not fully aware of the risks involved by the processing, and later wants to remove such personal data, especially on the internet. The data subject should be able to exercise that right notwithstanding the fact that he or she is no longer a child. However, the further retention of the personal data should be lawful where it is necessary, for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information, for compliance with a legal obligation, for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, on the grounds of public interest in the area of public health, for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims. 
>
> (66) To strengthen the right to be forgotten in the online environment, the right to erasure should also be extended in such a way that a controller who has made the personal data public should be obliged to inform the controllers which are processing such personal data to erase any links to, or copies or replications of those personal data. In doing so, that controller should take reasonable steps, taking into account available technology and the means available to the controller, including technical measures, to inform the controllers which are processing the personal data of the data subject's request.
>
> (67) Methods by which to restrict the processing of personal data could include, inter alia, temporarily moving the selected data to another processing system, making the selected personal data unavailable to users, or temporarily removing published data from a website. In automated filing systems, the restriction of processing should in principle be ensured by technical means in such a manner that the personal data are not subject to further processing operations and cannot be changed. The fact that the processing of personal data is restricted should be clearly indicated in the system.
</details>

this needs to be made a higher priority. it's getting to the point where we're seeing admins less active or abandoning instances, and users should not be expected to delegate this level of control of their accounts to absent admins, or admins who end up being untrustworthy or hacked. (I'd also like to reiterate the legal requirement, and "just ask the admin to do it" really isn't going to cut it as anything more than an immediate bandaid for the very immediate future.) 

i've got an account on an instance that appears to be losing the admin's interest, and is a few versions behind with no response from the admins, and while i'm okay with waiting awhile to see what happens, it's getting to the point where i'm thinking about when i should worry that the admin doesn't have control of a server any more, or if there will ever be a point when there are security concerns as a result of an instance/server being a few versions behind.

i understand this is more complex than i can fully appreciate as an end-user who doesn't code, but that doesn't change the fact that this is an incredibly important fundamental need and something users deserve.

a potential first step might be (again, i say this as a non-coder) the ability for a user to remove their data from a server in one fell swoop, with the understanding that toots that have been propagated out into the fediverse may not be recalled (this is not unlike sending an email to someone and then deleting the email account: the emails don't disappear, but i can't reply to or look up that account once it's been deleted). a username could be frozen and never reused, or reused only after a set period of time (a month, 6 months, whatever).

that doesn't necessarily meet all the requirements of the EU's right to disappear, but i reiterate the email account example. a user @yahoo.co.uk's email account doesn't recall and delete all previously sent emails, but they can certainly delete the actual account and everything hosted by that domain.

Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately. Issue body: Dataverse violates the GDPR because it doesn't ask the user for consent before sending visitor information to Google Tag Manager and setting a cookie on the visitor's browser. You should use some kind of popup to ask for consent, and only then load the Google Tag Manager. For example, a popup like this works very well: https://github.com/chiiya/haven/ I noticed this behavior in Dataverse 5.2, but I suppose it's the same in all. Issue discussion: Comment 1 | created 2021-01-04T15:45:11Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754050786 Hi @alanorth, thanks for creating this issue. This is a Dataverse-installation specific issue, as some installations may not be subject to GDPR. There are some installations that provide the workflow that you describe (ex. https://data.aussda.at/) and it would be interesting to figure out if there's some opportunity for adding common code to https://github.com/gdcc for installations that need to support GDPR (for those installations that are subject to it). cc: @qqmyers @skasberger Comment 2 | created 2021-01-04T20:41:31Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754206666 @djbrooke to be frank: we shouldn't be sending information about our users to third parties without their consent—whether we are subject to GDPR or not. It's just the right thing to do! As for a solution: I am not well versed in the Dataverse ecosystem, though I don't think we should need any custom code. We only need to replace the explicit call to Google Analytics to one that asks the user before setting cookies or sending hits. The [solution I linked](https://github.com/chiiya/haven/) is JavaScript and you literally just need to include it. Does Dataverse make site configuration available programmatically? If so, then you can template the JavaScript initiation to substitute the analytics ID, popup message, link etc that the site admin would configure in settings. P.S. the popup at aussdata.at is a bad example in my opinion because it uses jargon, dark patterns, and is too complex. We should be using _very_ simple language with an easy option to reject. Do you remember how GitHub did it for a few days in 2020-12, which only lasted a few days until they [abandoned the popup altogether](https://github.blog/2020-12-17-no-cookie-for-you/)? They said "We are going to track you. Is that OK? Yes / No." Here's a good example on our [academic repository](https://cgspace.cgiar.org/). It really doesn't have to be complicated... Comment 3 | created 2021-01-04T21:41:29Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754236879 Thanks @alanorth for the detailed response. If it's discussion about best practice vs. GDPR violation can you update the title to reflect this? A few thoughts: - Over the last few releases, the project has made some good progress in making it easier to programmatically configure (thanks to @poikilotherm), so this may be an opportunity to use those newfound powers. - As you mention, there are varying opinions on what should and should not be in that popup. This highlights why this is such a challenging area to work in and meet the needs across the various community use cases, and why we're pushing these decisions down to the individual installations - I know you mentioned GA specifically, but I wonder if Make Data Count and Matomo also need some consideration here, since Dataverse supports integration with both. It'll be good to get some additional thoughts here. Thanks again! Comment 4 | created 2021-01-04T21:58:53Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754245921 @alanorth thanks for bringing this issue to our attention. Dataverse installations have complete control over the code for Google Analytics (or other services like Matomo). We ask installations to put the code in a file called "analytics-code.html" and then configure Dataverse to use it. I'll include a screenshot of the details below from https://guides.dataverse.org/en/5.3/installation/config.html#web-analytics-code That said, I'm wondering what the "definition of done" is for this issue. Should the Dataverse guides suggest that Haven tool you mentioned? Should the guides provide some guidance on GDPR generally? Like @djbrooke said, some installations of Dataverse such as https://data.aussda.at have cookie warnings (screenshot below). Again, I think we don't get a lot of complaints about this because there's a lot of flexibility in what installations put in that analytics-code.html file (as well as the header and the footer). Comment 5 | created 2021-01-04T23:49:46Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754293341 We at AUSSDA pass the cookie snippet as custom header. In general, it would be great to have an own endpoint for this, cause the order of Javascript calls is relevant for this. Cookiebot for example must be the first call in . Matomo does not matter as far as i know. Comment 6 | created 2021-01-05T11:01:21Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754566009 > Dataverse installations have complete control over the code for Google Analytics (or other services like Matomo). We ask installations to put the code in a file called "analytics-code.html" and then configure Dataverse to use it. @pdurbin Ah! I did not know that. I will tell my site admin to look into it. I think this issue can be closed.
My personal opinion is that GDPR (or CCPA, etc) compliance doesn't have to be hard if you honestly respect your users. Most web developers and or project managers simply do not understand, do not care, or use adblockers since 2002. The compliance popups that have become the norm are abhorrent because they are purposefully confusing with dark patterns and language. I am a computer scientist with thirty+ years on the Internet and _even I_ have to read them carefully. There should be a simple "reject" option at the very front. And until the user actively consents you should not send a page hit or set a cookie. It's the right thing to do. Dataverse is in the realm of open source, open data, open government, academic research, etc... not startups and for-profit corporations. Sorry. ;) Comment 7 | created 2021-01-05T14:27:28Z Source: https://github.com/IQSS/dataverse/issues/7496#issuecomment-754668226 Thanks @alanorth for kicking off the discussion, I'll close this. As I mentioned and @pdurbin better explained, we allow the configuration so that individual installations can make the decisions that are right for them and their users.

Issue body:
## Overview

Depends on #636

To allow reporting on API usage, log all requests made with an API token to the database.

### Describe the solution you'd like
- Create a `RequestLog` table
  - ~`requested_at`~ `created_at` timestamp (opted to reuse our conventional timestamp field name)
  - `user_id` FK to api_user, indexed, cascade delete
  - `token` indexed ~(both alone and compound index with user_id)~ (Opting to not add speculatively add a multicolumn index) NOT an FK because tokens can be rotated.
  - `url` string
  - `response_code` int
- Create middleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/2.2/topics/http/middleware/#writing-your-own-middleware) that writes a row to the table if an API request is made with a token


Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2019-06-27T12:57:07Z
Source: https://github.com/opensupplyhub/open-apparel-registry/issues/637#issuecomment-506334505
Do we have a sense for how many requests this will be? Surfacing minor concern over the possibility of:

- Adding functionality that could lead to a large database table (over time)
- Introduces a step in the request/response cycle that has the potential to compromise the success of a request if this particular step fails

Comment 2 | created 2019-06-27T17:57:45Z
Source: https://github.com/opensupplyhub/open-apparel-registry/issues/637#issuecomment-506448828
Thanks for raising these concerns. 

We don't know just how successful our APIs will be, but we are actively engaged with multi-supplier initiatives to build integrations with their systems. I would guess the order of magnitude would be thousands per week.

We are obligated to report on API usage to our stakeholders, so we need to keep a count somewhere. I don't think we can avoid introducing a step in the request/response cycle, but I would definitely want to implement it so that a failure to count does not fail the request. 

I'm open to using an alternate data store. We don't need real time access to these counts so that could give us some flexibility.

One advantage to using the database is that we can maintain a foreign key to the user table and cascade delete when and if a user exercises their "right to be forgotten" under the GDPR.

Comment 3 | created 2019-07-02T02:07:06Z
Source: https://github.com/opensupplyhub/open-apparel-registry/issues/637#issuecomment-507489216
Thanks for the follow-up. Not super interested in pursuing an alternate data store at this time. GDPR makes it difficult to use the existing logging structure, which would have been great to reuse. I guess we just need to keep an eye on the size of this table over time.

Issue body:
When using a KML overlay, OpenLayers is making an unexpected request to https://maps.google.com/mapfiles/kml/pushpin/ylw-pushpin.png, even though this file is nowhere referenced in my KML file. I even do not use any points at all, that might justify loading a generic marker image as default icon style.

Because the path to the map in my current project also contains somewhat confidential data, and this is getting sent to Google via the Referer header field, this behavior is not just an unnecessary request, but a data leak/privacy issue.

My proposal: If there is no marker used, there should be no request. If the KML file uses a marker with no explicit icon href, a local file should be used as the default icon to prevent this unexpected data leak. Hardcoding a remote image URI like in the current version of OpenLayers also causes unnecessary dependencies. If somebody wants to use the Google marker icon from the current location, one could specify it in the style.

Scope: Retrieval-time original issue/comment Markdown from GitHub's structured page data; full discussion only when count and pagination checks pass. Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately.

Issue body:
### User story
As a user of the `smartnoise-synth` library, I frequently want to anonymize personally identifiable information (PII) in the data.

### Detailed description
To prevent leakage of sensitive information PII is anonymized by an analyst when preprocessing the data. Generating fake data is a solution because it discards existing values and instead uses entirely new ones. The most popular library for this is [Faker](https://pypi.org/project/Faker).

### Proposed solution
One possibility would be to follow the idea of the Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) [implementation](https://github.com/sdv-dev/SDV/discussions/667). It integrates `Faker` and allows a user to pass an `anonymize_fields` keyword argument. This maps a column to a corresponding provider. Even though that is quite user-friendly, it restricts the usage of more complex generation ideas, e.g. providing a custom implementation.

Therefore, I suggest not to integrate `Faker` directly, but instead let the user pass a function for generating fake data. Since data transforms can be provided in a `TableTransformer` object, I suggest implementing a new `ColumnTransformer` class for anonymization.

Feel free to make suggestions. I will implement the functionality soon.



Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2022-11-20T17:51:19Z
Source: https://github.com/opendp/smartnoise-sdk/issues/505#issuecomment-1321200323
That's a great idea.  I think it's OK to take a dependency on faker for their built-ins, but I also like the idea of allowing overrides.  As you suggest, this should be possible by deriving `snsynth.transform.base.ColumnTransformer` .  Since it will be assuming the column is PII, it shouldn't be necessary to implement anything for `_fit`, just for `_transform` and `_inverse_transform`.  Presumably the `_transform` just scrubs the value, and `_inverse_transform` generates fake PII when reversing the transform.

The current `ColumnTransformer` design allows `_transform` to map from 1 to n columns, with `_inverse_transform` mapping back from n to 1.  I'm not entirely sure the best way to handle this with, for example, a single column of PII.  Conceptually, the whole PII column is dropped, but then we have nothing to invert back (we can't map 1-->0 and then 0<--1).  An easy choice would be for `_transform` on the anonymizing `ColumnTransformer` to emit a column of `None` that the `TableTransformer` can then ignore when feeding the synthesizers (and re-inject on reverse transform).  So, the anonymizing column transformer would only emit the column of `None` when operating standalone or in a `ChainTransformer`.

Of course, I am assuming that the synthesizers don't want to train on fake PII, so it's best to drop those inbound and add the fakes outbound.  However, there might be cases where someone wants to replace real PII with fakes in both directions, in which case `_transform` could add fakes.

I'm assuming some of the more common types of PII could be specified when creating the column transformer:

```python
anon = TheNewColumnTransformer(some_prop_to_specify_fake_type='email')
assert(anon.fit_complete)
scrubbed = anon.transform(my_email_list)
reversed_emails = anon.inverse_transform(scrubbed)
assert(len(reversed_emails) == len(my_email_list))
```

And then maybe that could also take a caller-provided function per your proposal?

If you get the `ColumnTransformer` implemented, I can plug it in to `TableTransformer` and the data type inference stuff.  This would actually unblock a feature we want to add for SQL as well, so we can auto-generate metadata.

Issue body:
The Pwned Passwords (https://haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords) website recently upgraded to version 2 (https://www.troyhunt.com/ive-just-launched-pwned-passwords-version-2/) and 1Password provided integration with that service almost immediately. KeePassXC could provide similar levels of feedback to users on the 'quality' of their passwords.

When the user chooses to provide their own password (or uses an existing one), KeePassXC can check against the Pwned Passwords database (online/offline?) to see if the user provided password has been used in a previous data breach, and then provide a warning if it has. The 'k-Anonymity' feature would seem to be the one to use.

This lack of a 'fix' to this issue does not directly affect me (or anyone else) negatively, but it could encourage users to better password hygiene. It might soon become a 'benchmark feature' that all good password managers include.

Comment 1 | created 2018-03-02T14:55:49Z
Source: https://github.com/keepassxreboot/keepassxc/issues/1597#issuecomment-369942583
We already discussed this in #1083 and after that we made a blog post about it https://keepassxc.org/blog/2018-02-24-pwned-database/

The better password hygiene should be: "generate random password and store them in a password manager", not "come up with a password that wasn't already compromised"

Anyway, checking if an account has been compromised (not pwned password but haveibeenpwned) is tracked by #551

Comment 2 | created 2018-03-02T14:57:04Z
Source: https://github.com/keepassxreboot/keepassxc/issues/1597#issuecomment-369942939
This database is pretty useless if you are using a password manager. If you are using a good password, the only realistic chance of your password being in there is if a) your account was hacked AND b) the service saved your password as clear text.

Checking your username against the haveibeenpwned username database is way more useful. If your password is in the Pwned dump, it's almost certain that your username will be in the database, too. On the other hand, if your account was hacked and the service properly hashed your password, you won't notice if you only check if your password is in the database.

Comment 3 | created 2018-03-02T15:11:32Z
Source: https://github.com/keepassxreboot/keepassxc/issues/1597#issuecomment-369947119
I would not say that it's pretty useless - you are assuming two things:

1. Users will _always_ use the random password generator - they might not, for whatever reasons (novice users, etc).
2. Users are starting with a brand new, fresh password database. It is possible that they are importing an old password database from another manager, and have not performed any password hygiene on their pre-existing passwords. 

In addition, having that functionality easily available is useful for other reasons beyond your own personal password security. You could use the feature to demonstrate to family/friends that _their_ passwords are NOT secure. A bit like having a stand-alone random password generate is sometimes useful for reasons beyond generating a password for a website.

Anyway, I obviously hadn't realised that you'd already considered using this service (my search wasn't very thorough!), so I'll not say any more apart from to re-iterate that there are more use cases / user stories than the most obvious (and probably redundant) one.

Anyway, as I said: checking your password against a database is just plain useless. Even if you are using a bad password, you will ONLY find it in the database if the hacked service did not hash and salt your password.
Check your username instead. You will always find it, no matter if the hacked service did their homework on password security or not.

### Used Zammad Version

5.3; 5.x; 4.x

### Environment

- Installation method: [any
- Operating system (if you're unsure: `cat /etc/os-release` ): any
- Database + version: any
- Elasticsearch version: any
- Browser + version: any


### Actual behaviour

Zammad never forgets about the data privacy tasks admins added.
This may lead into extremely huge views causing possible performance degrade in the affected UI part.

Also this kind of means data hoarding - should behave similar to other data potions:
https://docs.zammad.org/en/latest/appendix/privacy.html

### Expected behaviour

Zammad cleans up data privacy tasks on a regular basis. Like 6 months and older or so.

### Steps to reproduce the behaviour

Create data privacy tasks, let them run and come back after years.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6549061/208648717-2c0fdf10-5f1e-4ac4-b0ce-e2ce9d32177c.png)

_No response_

no

Comment 1 | created 2023-01-30T08:00:51Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1408143612
Since deleting data should always be done with great caution, I think 6 months is too short here. Customer projects often last longer than half a year, which means you still need the chance to have a look where tickets are. Therefore this time frame seems a bit too short to me. Suggestion: 12 months. 

Comment 2 | created 2023-03-02T15:24:58Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452052645
Can this be enabled/disabled or can the timeframe be configured?

Comment 3 | created 2023-03-02T15:28:51Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452058888
No, but you could create a cronjob or run it manually if you want to run it more often.

`zammad run rails r "DataPrivacyTask.cleanup(1.month)"` 

This command would clean up tasks created older than 1 month if you run it daily via cronjob.

Comment 4 | created 2023-03-02T15:40:55Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452076919
Oh, that's nifty. Thank you for the feedback.

Is there also a solution for clients that want to have the data for more than 12 months, for example for 5 years?

Comment 5 | created 2023-03-02T15:51:27Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452093219
Not really. You could completely disable it:

`Scheduler.find_by(method: 'DataPrivacyTask.cleanup').update(active: false)`


Comment 6 | created 2023-03-02T15:53:18Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452096167
Alternatively, if these requirements often come to you, then it might make sense to think about a setting to configure it in the core.

Comment 7 | created 2023-03-02T15:54:50Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1452098583
> Not really. You could completely disable it:
> 
> Scheduler.find_by(method: 'DataPrivacyTask.cleanup').update(active: false)

Please don't this. This is not a recommended action and shouldn't be a a recommendation at all.


Comment 8 | created 2023-03-03T10:30:40Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1453309669
Without a setting (which is "off" per default), I personally consider this a breaking change. With this update, we will destroy client data, that may be needed by some of them. And as the whole function may be relevant in legal cases, we should reconsider activating this per default.

Comment 9 | created 2023-03-03T14:07:52Z
Source: https://github.com/zammad/zammad/issues/4437#issuecomment-1453585175
This scheduler task is about old dataprivacy tasks **after** they deleted data.
Imho technically the old ticket numbers don't help you too much as you don't know who the obscured user is anyway.

I don't see any legal issues at this point.
Feel free to contact me directory on this Gerrit, I believe this is a missunderstanding.

Issue body:
Currently, for downloading the favicon of a website we are relying on Google by doing the following trick,

``` c++
QString path = "http://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=" + url.host();
```

This though doesn't work with some websites, with [packagist.org](http://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=packagist.org) being such an example. For finding the favicon a typical web browser first checks the HTML code of the web page for one of the following tags,

``` html
<link rel="shortcut icon" href="http://example.com/myicon.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/vnd.microsoft.icon" href="http://example.com/image.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/x-icon" href="http://example.com/image.ico">
<link rel="icon" href="http://example.com/image.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/gif"  href="http://example.com/image.gif">
<link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="http://example.com/image.png">
```

If neither of those are being found, then the web browser checks if the file `favicon.ico` exists on the root of the website. So, to do it properly we first need to download the HTML code, parse it in order to find one or more of those tags, try to fetch the favicon based on them and if it is unsuccessful try to fetch the `favicon.ico` file from the root of the website.

If you agree with this I can take a look to see if I can implement this, so we can make the download of the favicon more robust and we won't have to rely on Google for something like that, which might actually stop working in the future and break that functionality of the application.
#30

I'm not so sure about the necessity of this. If I wanted to remove EXIF data, I could get an app that does it, and send the stripped version. Otherwise I would want to send the photo with EXIF data, if I want my recipient to know where and when it was taken, and the aperture, shutter speed, etc. Maybe it could be optional in the app? 

On a side note if we want Signal to be sending completely "anonymous photos", we should definitely be considering the issue of [camera fingerprinting](https://33bits.org/2011/09/19/digital-camera-fingerprinting/) as well. Without making special modifications to a photo, the subtle imperfections of a photo can be used to identify the camera that took it. For example, if you use your phone's camera to take pictures that you post publicly on Facebook, and send a different photo from the same camera to a person anonymously, camera fingerprinting based on the contents of the actual photo could be used to tie the anonymous photo to your Facebook identity, without checking EXIF data.

Source: https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-iOS/issues/1984#issuecomment-353191260
For iOS, the current logic is that in order to avoid re-encoding GIF/PNGs as JPEG we are retrieving the raw data using the Photo Framework (`PHAsset` instead of using `UIImagePickerControllerOriginalImage`), which happens to include EXIF and GPS data with it.

So, in order to keep the current functionality and code as is, one option available would be to add an extra step - after retrieving that `NSData` from the Photo Framework,
remove the `kCGImagePropertyExifDictionary` and `kCGImagePropertyGPSDictionary` from it. This will remove all the EXIF and GPS data before sending the image. Because the data returned from the Photo Framework is immutable, a copy of the data with the stripped attributes would have to be made.

This is something I could implement and do a PR for, unless anyone has any objections to that solution or better suggestions here.

Issue body:
Please stop updating GDevelop automatically.
Instead, prompt a message saying a new update is available and let me decide if I want to download it and install it.
Or, add an option to let me choose if I want GDevelop to update automatically or not.

It would be also important for security. If you release something broken that is going to corrupt my project file let me decide if I do want to take that risk or not. Project file can be corrupted also if GD crash while in use and write the project file since you are developing GDevelop on a Mac that only 1% of people using, there is no way for you to be sure everything is ok on Windows. Also in case your GtHub get hacked, currently it would be very simple to infect all GD5 users with virus and malware. Since you also take subscriptions in-app, I guess you don't want peoples card details being compromised as the direct result of this unsafe approach of updating GDevelop.

The bottom line is, for security reasons let me decide what do I want download and run.

Also, you did mentioned something about collecting crash reports and usage data automatically. If you have that in, let me turn that off too for the very same reasons. It can be exploited by viruses and malware and I don't care about how secure it is, the bottom line is, let me take full control what GDevelop doing on my computer.
.
Thanks.

Project: joomla/joomla-cms

Scope: Retrieval-time original issue/comment Markdown from GitHub's structured page data; full discussion only when count and pagination checks pass. Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately.

Issue body:
### Steps to reproduce the issue

* Enable the System - Privacy Consent plugin
* Log in to the frontend of the site as a user who has not yet provided consent
* You are redirected to the profile edit page
* Change any field but do NOT touch the consent (Privacy Policy) - leave it to No
* Click on Save

### Expected result

Nothing is saved because I have not provided my consent.

### Actual result

Changes are saved, including in third party plugin fields which ask for personally identifiable information such as phone numbers, addresses etc. This is a direct violation of the GDPR. You are storing my personally identifiable information with me having explicitly declined my consent!

### System information (as much as possible)

Joomla! 3.9.0. Everything else is absolutely irrelevant.

### Additional comments

Obviously you could say that com_users should not save anything unless the Privacy Policy field is submitted and is set to Yes. There are some gotchas, both architectural and UX.

The only _reasonable_ way to fix it is to implement a captive login for consent using its own, special view in com_users which is the only view accessible without providing consent.

results.document: Released issue metadata: Issue title: Google Analytics internal template doesn't interact with cookie consent Project: gohugoio/hugo Issue type: issue Matched keywords: "['privacy problem', 'cookie law']" GitHub labels: ["Stale", "EmbeddedTemplate", "Outdated"] Status in release: closed Comments in release: 7; discussants: 3 Reported: 2021-02-19 09:00:19+00; last active: 2022-05-21 02:02:05+00 Issue number: 8262 Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 7/7 Scope: Retrieval-time original issue/comment Markdown from GitHub's structured page data; full discussion only when count and pagination checks pass. Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately. Issue body: In the current implementation of the Google Analytics internal template, there seems to be no way to disable analytics based on user preference through a "cookie consent" interface. These are increasingly common, and it would be nice if there were a way for the internal template to honour a runtime request not to set cookies. At the moment the template allows for the honouring of a browser Do Not Track preference, and the entire code is wrapped in a `doNotTrack` boolean. That completely prevents the use of analytics for users who set this browser preference, which is fantastic. However, so far as I can tell there's no way to influence the value of this variable from outside the template. And there's (understandably) no way for javascript to toggle the browser DNT preference. Issue discussion: Comment 1 | created 2021-02-22T18:49:20Z Source: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/8262#issuecomment-783592031 I believe you can turn on `useSessionStorage` to [disable the use of cookies](https://gohugo.io/about/hugo-and-gdpr/#googleanalytics). But I haven't tested this myself and I'm not sure if this is even GDPR compliant. You should note that Google Analytics v4 doesn't support disabling cookies at all. #8264 As for consent. What about using localStorage. You would need to set `doNotTrack` to true before GA loads then remove it after consent. ```js if (!doNotTrack && !localStorage.getItem("doNotTrack")) { ... } ``` Comment 2 | created 2021-02-23T14:51:56Z Source: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/8262#issuecomment-784257032 Unfortunately, whether you use local storage or cookies doesn't change the "cookie consent" problem, at least not from a privacy law perspective. The underlying directive covers all forms of storage. So this isn't really about disabling cookies so much as allowing users to opt-out of tracking at run time. Your idea of using localStorage could provide a workaround, but the existing internal template would need to be amended to allow for that since it current (as of the v0.80.0 snap) generates Javascript code that reads: ``` var dnt = (navigator.doNotTrack || window.doNotTrack || navigator.msDoNotTrack); var doNotTrack = (dnt == "1" || dnt == "yes"); if (!doNotTrack) { ... ``` which I can't manipulate from outside the template. Comment 3 | created 2021-02-23T18:14:59Z Source: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/8262#issuecomment-784405447 I just realized that there is no need for template changes. `doNotTrack` is a global variable that you can modify yourself. ```html {{ template "_internal/google_analytics.html" . }} ``` Update the localstorage item after consent, reload the page and you should be good to go. This works because `var doNotTrack` is the exact same variable as `window.doNotTrack`. I've only tested it a little bit but it looks like it should work in Chrome, Safari, and Firefox. Comment 4 | created 2021-02-24T08:27:38Z Source: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/8262#issuecomment-784900706 Oh, that's a clever side effect of the choice of variable name, and something I'd not cottoned onto. I guess it also relies on the fact that the `var doNotTrack = (dnt == "1" || dnt == "yes");` assignment doesn't change the existing value of doNotTrack if dnt is undefined. So maybe the substance of this issue should be to document that since it's non-obvious to people who only occasionally dabble in javascript (I asked several people before opening the issue :)). Comment 5 | created 2021-02-24T16:27:28Z Source: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/issues/8262#issuecomment-785199140 I agree that it should be documented. I'll see what I can come up with later this week. Issue body:
Dear all, 

during my attempts to bidsify some eeg data, I stumbled on some points that are not clear for me. Could you please clarify them for me?

1. Should the labels of session, acquisition and run be consistent between subjects? 
   - I couldn't find this in the specification, but validator suggests that each subject should have exactly the same set of sessions and acquisitions.
2. Are the fields in events.tsv can be picked only from given table, or I can define my own (with corresponding entry into json)?
   - In doc it says "The tabular files consists of one row per event and a set of REQUIRED and OPTIONAL columns". This suggests that I can choose only from the given fields, but if it's fixed I still need to define labels in json. If other labels are allowed, can you mention it in document?
3. Can you clarify the policy of anonymization? 
   - In description of scans.tsv you require the shift of dates by a fixed amount of days. This implies that the scan date must be also removed from the data file, but   I didn't found it mentioned explicitly. Moreover, EDF format requires an entry of a date -- should it be the same date as in scans.tsv, or I can choose a fixed fake one?

Thanks in advance 


Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2019-03-28T15:12:23Z
Source: https://github.com/bids-standard/bids-specification/issues/194#issuecomment-477638077
Not an exhaustive answer, but a start:

Answer to q1
--------------
Can you clarify your question with the use case that you are working on?

I just answer in how far I understand your question for now. "You should be consistent with your labels". I.e., you have two participants in your study, participant 1 had two sessions, and participant 2 had only one session (e.g., because they were sick that day, or the budget was empty, ...)

Then it'd be sensible to call the session labels
- `sub-1_ses-1` and `sub-1_ses-2` for participant 1 ... and
- `sub-2_ses-1` for participant 2

so the labels are consistent, but it is not required that they are equal (because that's sometimes just not the case)


Answer to q2
--------------
You can define your own columns if they are documented in an accompanying JSON file. See the [spec](https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/04-modality-specific-files/05-task-events.html):

> An arbitrary number of additional columns can be added. Those allow describing other properties of events 

this is documented slightly below the phrase that you quote. But if you think the documentation should be improved with a slight twist of wording, feel free to send a PR!

I'm sorry to come back to this acquisition again and again, I'm responsible for bidsifying in laboratory, so I try eliminate any double interpretation and still keep it convenient for us. Moreover, the conversion is intended to happen in automatic workflow, without manual labeling of samples.

>Using time of acquisition as as the value of acq is not following it's intended use. It is suppose to distinguish different types of acquisition

I'm aware of it, and it will be changed for sure. In our case sometimes we have 2 eeg similar scans for same subject and acquisition label is a natural way to distinguish them. The time was used to this goal before the bids era -- so we just kept same labeling.

> We are trying to clarify it with @robertoostenveld in #173 and this google doc

In my naive interpretation, an acquisition is one full session of acquisition data (i.e. one eeg file). If experiment expect only one acquisition per task, then there are no label, and if there a possibility to have several per task, then acq label becomes mandatory.

And then, if one acquisition (one file) can be split into segments, these becomes runs. It fits nicely "uninterrupted repetition of data acquisition".

Please tell me if it is a reasonable interpretation.

Comment 6 | created 2019-04-06T07:07:09Z
Source: https://github.com/bids-standard/bids-specification/issues/194#issuecomment-480480719
Sorry for getting back to you so late @nbeliy. I'll try to make up for it with an exhaustive answer.

Have you taken a look at the [definitions](https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/02-common-principles.html#definitions) part of the specification?

> **Data acquisition** - a continuous uninterrupted block of time during which a brain scanning instrument was acquiring data according to particular scanning sequence/protocol.

> **Run** - an uninterrupted repetition of data acquisition that has the same acquisition parameters and task (however events can change from run to run due to different subject response or randomized nature of the stimuli). Run is a synonym of a data acquisition.

Given these definitions, your naive interpretation of a data acquisition is correct: One full uninterrupted data recording. Note however, that data acquisition in this sense is DISTINCT from the `acq` parameter (I'll come to that below).

Your second comment that splitting one acquisition into segments would mean having several runs is a bit misguided as far as I can see. With our definitions, data acquisitions and runs are synonymous ... you can say: This data is from acquisition 1 ... or this data is from run 1 (it means the same).

Dividing a data recording into segments AFTER the acquisition sounds like a derivative to me, which is not yet completely defined - please see [BEP021](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PmcVs7vg7Th-cGC-UrX8rAhKUHIzOI-uIOh69_mvdlw/edit?disco=AAAACoSruhQ&usp_dm=false&ts=5c811e55)

Now having that sorted out, let's come back to the `acq` parameter.

This is defined [here (scroll down a bit)](https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/04-modality-specific-files/01-magnetic-resonance-imaging-data.html#anatomy-imaging-data):

> The OPTIONAL acq-<label> key/value pair corresponds to a custom label the user MAY use to distinguish a different set of parameters used for acquiring the same modality. For example this should be used when a study includes two T1w images - one full brain low resolution and and one restricted field of view but high resolution.

With regards to an EEG recording, the `acq` parameter makes little (or none at all) sense, because unlike with a T1w MRI scan, we are not measuring a "stable configuration" (e.g., distribution of white and grey matter in the brain) but a "dynamic process" (e.g., postsynaptic potentials). And we can never re-measure that past dynamic process with a different set of acquisition parameters.

### Example (I know you are working with sleep data, so let me try):

- measure EEG in first hour after going to bed on the 4th of May 2018 using `acq-1000fs` (the label could mean sampling rate 1000 for the EEG)

- Now try do do a `acq-250fs` --> it's impossible, because time has passed and the EEG activity of the first hour after going to bed on the 4th of May 2018 will never return


The `acq` parameter CAN be meaningfully used in EEG.

### Example:

- You are using the Nasion, Left, and Right Periaruicular Points as reference points for electrode locations (NAS, LPA, RPA)
- To communicate the exact position of NAS, LPA, and RPA, you make photos of the participant (see [here](https://bids-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/04-modality-specific-files/03-electroencephalography.html#landmark-photos-_photojpg) for an example)
- The photo showing the Nasion could be called `sub-0001_ses-001_acq-NAS_photo.jpg`
- The photo of the Right Periauricular Point could be called `sub-0001_ses-001_acq-RPA_photo.jpg`

... strictly speaking these are not different acquisition parameters (i.e., the settings of the camera are probably the same) - but it would be a valid "re-use" of the acq parameter.

Released issue metadata:
Issue title: Use asymmetric encryption
Project: padloc/padloc
Issue type: issue
Matched keywords: "['data breach']"
GitHub labels: []
Status in release: closed
Comments in release: 12; discussants: 2
Reported: 2016-11-07 15:36:19+00; last active: 2018-05-24 07:18:56+00
Issue number: 57

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 12/12
Scope: Retrieval-time original issue/comment Markdown from GitHub's structured page data; full discussion only when count and pagination checks pass. Closure time is not available from this endpoint. Linked material is stored separately.

Issue body:
IDK if this is a real issue or not, but I was thinking about it this morning

It seems like the architecture is that the DB file is symmetrically encrypted using the passphrase I choose and stored on the server to be synchronized with other devices

That means if someone gets ahold of my database file somehow (e.g. back end server breach) they could relatively easily brute force or dictionary attack passwords on the file unless my passphrase was very complicated (and I doubt most people have complicated passphrases)

Seems like padlock should be using public key encryption where each machine has its own key pair and the key pair has a passphrase-allows you to use different keyphrases on different machines as well. The only limitation of that approach is that a machine with access to the file has to be used to approve adding another device, because it would have to decrypt the file and re-encrypt with a new set of public keys

LMK if I'm totally off base here (I'm hoping that I am)

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2016-11-07T16:54:50Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258892567
Brute-force and dictionary attacks are real concerns but there are steps we are taking to mitigate the risks. Basically it comes down to using the right method for key derivation. We're using [PBKDF2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBKDF2), which uses a method called [key stretching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_stretching) to make these kind of attacks harder. Of course, the reality is that an attacker with sufficient resources might still be able to break the encryption within a finite amount of time but using the methods mentioned above, we can make it uneconomical for an attacker to even try (i.e. it would take years and millions of dollars to break the encryption, even with a moderately strong password). Of course, making sure that users are using a sufficiently strong password is still a big concern. But that is what the strength-meter and the warning for weak passwords at the getting started screen is for ;)

Aside from the fact that asymmetric encryption is not feasible for large amounts of data I don't see how your approach would make the encryption any more robust. Can you explain, for example, how it would protect against brute-force attacks?


Comment 2 | created 2016-11-07T17:22:16Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258900956
Hmm-I'd never heard of key stretching-that eases my concern a bit depending on how expensive it is to test a single passphrase against a DB file.

If you are using public key cryptography, the attacker would need both the DB file AND a private key from one of the connected devices to attempt to decrypt the file. It is completely impractical to generate a private key from the public keys for which the DB file is encrypted, and the server has no knowledge of the private keys. So a device has to be compromised in order for the DB files to be brute forced/dictionary attacked. How come you say it's not feasible to encrypt large amounts of data with public key encryption?


Comment 3 | created 2016-11-07T17:27:05Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258902301
PS I think iCloud keychain does something similar just based on the fact that it requires me to approve additional devices from other machines


Comment 4 | created 2016-11-07T17:34:24Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258904280
About why asymmetric crypto is not feasible for large amounts of data: http://crypto.stackexchange.com/a/5790


Comment 5 | created 2016-11-07T17:52:51Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258909268
It seems that's more of a performance/storage space concern-I wouldn't have any issue with waiting a few seconds for my db file to synchronize/decrypt/encrypt since it's not real time. I'm not sure what the average file size is for people's databases though. 

If necessary for performance though it's possible to use the suggested workaround of using asymmetric encryption to get at a long symmetric encryption key. The server would just have to store both the asymmetrically encrypted key and the symmetrically encrypted db file

Seems like a lot of work to change, but IMO it would be nice to know my data is totally safe from attack in case of a server breach


Comment 6 | created 2016-11-07T21:36:33Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258970456
> It seems that's more of a performance/storage space concern-I wouldn't have any issue with waiting a few seconds for my db file to synchronize/decrypt/encrypt since it's not real time.

I don't know how much longer it would take to encrypt the data with, say, rsa, but we're definitely talking about orders of magnitude here. It's quite possible that "a few seconds" won't be enough.

Also, if the data is encrypted with a device-specific public key and then stored on the server, how are other devices supposed to decrypt the data? Of course if every device knew the public key of every other device, it could upload an specifically encrypted version for each device but that leaves you with the fundamental problem of how to safely exchange public keys. And by the way, what makes you think that asymmetric crypto is not susceptible to brute-force attacks?


Comment 7 | created 2016-11-07T22:19:41Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-258981738
> I don't know how much longer it would take to encrypt the data with, say, rsa, but we're definitely talking about orders of magnitude here. It's quite possible that "a few seconds" won't be enough.

I was basing that guesstimate on the fact that symmetric algorithms were estimated to do 2000MB/s in that stackoverflow post, and asymmetric crypto being 5000 times slower- somewhere in the 0.5MB/s range-and my guess of my database file not being any larger than a MB (all I'm storing is textual data-but I'm not positive what other metadata is in that file)

> Also, if the data is encrypted with a device-specific public key and then stored on the server, how are other devices supposed to decrypt the data? 

It's encrypted with multiple device-specific public keys as recipients, so anyone with any of the corresponding device private keys can decrypt the file.

In order to add a device, a machine that has a working private key would have to decrypt the file and then re-encrypt it with the additional public key in addition to the existing public keys. AFAIK with GPG the encrypted file contains information about which public keys it was encrypted for. It should always be safe to exchange public keys-you could store the active public keys on the server and information about whether they have been incorporated into the DB file, so that a client can when it needs to authorize another device

Asymmetric crypto is technically susceptible to brute-force attacks, but a typical private key size is 2048 bits

EDIT disclaimer: I'm not at all experienced in cryptography, I've just used [GPG](https://www.gnupg.org/) enough to have a working knowledge of it


Comment 8 | created 2016-11-08T15:55:29Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-259175341
> Asymmetric crypto is technically susceptible to brute-force attacks, but a typical private key size is 2048 bits

I'm sure you know this, but due to the mathematical correlation between public and private key, a 2048 bit rsa key is roughly equivalent in strength to a (completely random) 128 bit aes key and using a larger key would likely not be practical due to performance concerns.

If I understand you correctly, your argument is that data encrypted using your technique would be less susceptible to key-guessing attacks due to a larger key space (because the 256 symmetric encryption keys are derived from the significantly smaller subset of passwords that can be handled by humans) but this is exactly what we're trying to mitigate through key stretching.

Its hard to say without running the numbers, but its quite possible that the encryption scheme you're suggesting would actually be **easier** to break than what we have now. More importantly though, it is significantly more **complicated** and arguably far from common practice. Don't get me wrong - I highly appreciate your input! But if there is one thing I've learned about cryptography, it's that it is usually best to stick to simple, battle tested patterns and common practice where possible. Crypto is hard enough to get right as it is without trying to come up with new solutions to already solved problems.

Btw, it's worth pointing out that I do see use cases for public key crypto in the future, specifically when it comes to sharing records between multiple accounts but for now I think it's best to stick with what we have.


Comment 9 | created 2016-11-08T16:23:41Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-259183757
> I'm sure you know this, but due to the mathematical correlation between public and private key, a 2048 bit rsa key is roughly equivalent in strength to a (completely random) 128 bit aes key and using a larger key would likely not be practical due to performance concerns.

Actually I didn't! Still, the bits are random so you don't have to worry about dictionary attacks. 

If an attacker got a hold of all the DB files, I would imagine the attacker would run a dictionary of common passwords through the key stretching algorithm, and then try each of the stretched keys against each of the databases. If you're doing key stretching in addition to salting, that would be less of a concern-but I didn't see that was mentioned.

edit: rainbow table - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_table

> If I understand you correctly, your argument is that data encrypted using your technique would be less susceptible to key-guessing attacks due to a larger key space (because the 256 symmetric encryption keys are derived from the significantly smaller subset of passwords that can be handled by humans) but this is exactly what we're trying to mitigate through key stretching.

It's less susceptible to key guessing because the key isn't determined by the user. The key is generated by the computer, and the user just picks a passcode on the device to unlock the key. The key is never shared with the server, so the attacker has to guess the longer private key instead of the user-selected passphrase. I can't imagine a scenario in which trying to guess a generated private key is easier to do than trying to guess a user-selected passphrase.

I do think it's a lot more complicated-but I also think this is what Apple does for iCloud keychain, so it's pretty safe to say it's the right way to share credentials between devices. See the iCloud keychain section here: https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT202303


Comment 10 | created 2016-11-09T12:47:06Z
Source: https://github.com/padloc/padloc/issues/57#issuecomment-259406827
> Still, the bits are random so you don't have to worry about dictionary attacks.

They aren't though. Key pairs are generated by solving a hard math problem the **parameters** of which are chose at random. This means that a asymmetric key of 2048 bits has **significantly** less entropy than a key of the same size in which every bit is chosen completely at random. It's true that dictionary attacks are not applicable to asymmetric key pairs but there are other techniques that are significantly more efficient than randomly guessing every single bit.

Anyway, I've heard your argument but I my decision remains to not change anything about the encryption scheme right now. I hope you don't mind if I close this issue now.

Issue body:
Hey guys,

I think it's kind of weird that DBeaver stores your database passwords in plain text in the .dbeaver-data-sources.xml file. That seems like a pretty big breach in data security. Am I wrong? Feels like the passwords should not be stored in that file, but seperately, hashed somewhere...

Comment 1 | created 2018-03-02T19:57:24Z
Source: https://github.com/dbeaver/dbeaver/issues/3066#issuecomment-370035514
DBeaver EE and DBeaver Eclipse plugin versions support passwords storage in secured database (encrypted with master password).
You can enable this in Preferences->Database->Security.

Regarding CE version:
Many users share database configurations so they need to keep password in the same configuration file (which is actually resides in some version control system).
But if your database passwords are secure then you can disable passwords save at all.

Note: password are saved not in plain text but in encrypted form (so you can't see them accidentally). But they can be easily decrypted with special software.

Comment 1 | created 2017-03-27T15:42:36Z
Source: https://github.com/Trustroots/trustroots/issues/485#issuecomment-289493805
Still WIP and messy. Already some insight.

https://onesignal.com/privacy_policy
https://onesignal.com/tos

_Disclaimer: I'm not a lawyer. I'm a dilletante. I don't fully understand the legal context of the research._

# TLDR

[onesignal.com](https://onesignal.com) collects a lot of data, including email addresses, location, behaviour, probably also the text of the notifications users receive. They try to label the users (i.e. sports fan if you're often around stadiums (how far can this go?)) and predict their behaviour.

They make money by selling the data to their Clients (i.e. to ad companies for making personalized advertising).

They will keep the data as long as they need to meet their purposes.

To say something nice: At least they are quite clear about their attitude in their Privacy Policy. With examples etc. They're rather foggy about it in their FAQ, though.

## The questions by @chmac 
- I haven't found any mentions about EU Law in Privacy Policy nor ToS.
- They don't force you to provide any info. They get the data when you use the service.
- I haven't found any promise to not sell personal info (look better?). On contrary they sell data i.e. so the clients may do targeted advertising. I'll look for more detail later.

## My impression?
I advise not to use this service. I would not choose them for my projects. I perceive them as Big Brother Service. However, i'm rather sensitive to this, so you better make your own judgement.

# Slightly more detail

_Users_ = us
_Clients_ = brands, ad companies, the ones who pay

- They collect email addresses, location (mobile location or IP address geolocation), all kinds of system information and configuration, unique identifiers, info about apps people use, how people interact with the apps (timestamps).
- They collect push notifications which people receive. Would this include the peoples' conversations from email notifications?
- They label users: i.e. if you're often near sport stadium, you'll become a "sport fan". (Isn't this one creepy?)
- They try to predict what users will do in future
- They or their clients (the ones who pay for the data) may connect the data, match ip addresses, email addresses and other info across devices etc.

- They say they generally hash the email addresses when they provide them to Clients, but don't promise they will.
- They don't promise anonymization.

# Detail with quoting (read the bold text for overview)

_SDK_ - software development kit
_End Users_ -  trustroots members
_Clients_ - onesignal's partners, advertisers, ... (the bodies who want the data)

## What they collect

### Web SDK
> - __Web pages visited__ that have implemented the SDK, and information about those visits (e.g., session duration, time-stamp, referring URLs)
> - What __push notifications__ an End User has been sent __(is this the actual text of notification, or not? I.e. text of the messages?)__
> - ... __transactions and interactions with apps and websites__
> __IP address__, from which __geographic location__ may be inferred, as well as system configuration information
> __Email address__ which we may (in our discretion) hash or otherwise deidentify __(they don't promise the deidentifying though!)__
> ... __browser [info]__, such as, browser language type and version of operating system (e.g., Android, iOS); network provider; language setting; time zone
> A __unique cookie identifier__, which may uniquely identify an End User (such as in de-identified or anonymous form).

### Mobile SDK

> __[installed] Apps__ ... [and some usage info]
> __Purchases__ made within an app.
> ... transactions and interactions with apps and websites
> __Mobile advertising identifiers__, such as iOS IDFAs and Android Advertising IDs (“Mobile IDs”). (They may associate these ids with other data.)
> __Precise Location information__, generally an End User’s lat/long data (i.e., GPS-level data) or WiFi information, which we may associate with Mobile IDs, and which may be collected whether or not an app is in use.
> __Email address__ ...
> __IP address__ ... [system configuration information]
> Information associated with or related to devices, such as device type (e.g., mobile, tablet); type and version of operating system (e.g., Android, iOS); network provider; mobile browser (e.g. Safari, Chrome, etc.); language setting; time zone; and network status type (such as WiFi).

Supplemental evidence: complete | comments retrieved 12/12
Scope: Retrieval-time original Markdown from GitHub's structured issue pages, including numbered timeline pages. Discussion complete only after pagination, comment-ID, expected-count and unchanged-issue checks. Closure timestamp is unavailable; linked material is stored separately.

Issue body:
Currently the SOCKS5 Server [drops TCP traffic](https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/blob/devel/Tribler/community/tunnel/Socks5/server.py#L191). In practice this means that all http trackers are unable to find peers. This can severely impact performance of some torrents.

To fix this, changes should be made to the following classes. These should forward TCP packets (probably using explicit subclassing for decoupling of TCP and UDP behaviors, [in line with the SOCKS5Connection](https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/blob/devel/Tribler/community/tunnel/Socks5/server.py#L25)):

- [The SOCKS5 connection](https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/blob/devel/Tribler/community/tunnel/Socks5/server.py#L104)
- [The exit node](https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/blob/devel/Tribler/community/tunnel/tunnel_community.py#L144)

An experimental implementation (by @devos50) already [exists](https://github.com/devos50/tribler/commit/71402bff2db51e2e14d671642907d6c9069de5d7) for reference. One possible backward compatible way to forward traffic is to use [conversion.is_allowed()](https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/blob/69445f0537d8e87bd01d2ca8bdc94a69c9819503/Tribler/community/tunnel/conversion.py#L553) to filter out UDP from TCP traffic.

EDIT: Only http trackers should be forwarded (not all TCP traffic), this reduces the chance of exit nodes being misused.

Issue discussion:
Comment 1 | created 2018-03-29T12:31:45Z
Source: https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/issues/2681#issuecomment-377220328
One possibility is to only support _get_peer_, hardcode the protocol that everything we DONT recognise would be filtered out. Talk UDP to the exit node and e.node talks TCP to tracker.
Or use SOCKS5 with filtering.
An explicit warning/error for connecting to HTTP-based trackers.

Comment 2 | created 2018-03-29T16:55:32Z
Source: https://github.com/Tribler/tribler/issues/2681#issuecomment-377301040
